# Estimators applied identically to simulated and observed data.
# y is log(estimate / true value); x is log(anchor / true value).

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(lme4); library(metafor); library(data.table) })

# Gross-error rule: drop responses further from the true value (log scale) than both a factor of
# 1,000 and ten times the most extreme anchor used for that cell. A response equal to any anchor
# is always retained, so the rule cannot remove strongly anchored answers.
drop_gross_errors <- function(dat) {
  dat <- dat[is.finite(y)]
  dat[, y_limit := pmax(log(1000), max(abs(x)) + log(10)), by = cell]
  dat[abs(y) <= y_limit][, y_limit := NULL][]
}

# Within-item response function: y = a_cell + b x + g x|x|, with uncorrelated random intercepts,
# slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by participant. b is the average elasticity at the true value; g > 0 means the
# local elasticity rises with anchor extremity, g < 0 means it falls.
fit_within <- function(dat) {
  dat <- drop_gross_errors(dat)
  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  m <- lmer(y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid), data = dat,
            control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE, check.conv.singular = "ignore"))
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  b <- co["x", "Estimate"]; g <- co["xx", "Estimate"]
  V <- as.matrix(vcov(m))[c("x", "xx"), c("x", "xx")]
  # Relative curvature rho = g / b, with a delta-method standard error.
  grad <- c(-g / b^2, 1 / b)
  list(model = m, b = b, b_se = co["x", "Std. Error"], g = g, g_se = co["xx", "Std. Error"],
       rho = g / b, rho_se = sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% V %*% grad)), n = nrow(dat))
}

# Across-cell anchoring index: log-scale index per two-anchor cell, meta-regressed on extremity
# (mean absolute log distance of the two anchors from the true value).
cell_indices <- function(rows, cells) {
  r <- merge(drop_gross_errors(rows)[, .(cell, anchorhigh, y)], cells[, .(cell, study, x_low, x_high, extremity)], by = "cell")
  r[, .(med_high = median(y[anchorhigh == 1]), med_low = median(y[anchorhigh == 0]),
        mad_high = mad(y[anchorhigh == 1]), mad_low = mad(y[anchorhigh == 0]),
        n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1), n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0),
        study = study[1], x_low = x_low[1], x_high = x_high[1], extremity = extremity[1]), by = cell][
    , `:=`(ai = (med_high - med_low) / (x_high - x_low),
           ai_se = 1.2533 * sqrt(pmax(mad_high, 1e-3)^2 / n_high + pmax(mad_low, 1e-3)^2 / n_low) / (x_high - x_low))][]
}

fit_across <- function(ci) {
  m <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci, method = "REML")
  list(model = m, slope = unname(coef(m)["extremity"]), slope_se = unname(m$se[2]),
       intercept = unname(coef(m)["intrcpt"]), mean_ai = weighted.mean(ci$ai, 1 / ci$ai_se^2))
}

PART 0
# Estimators applied identically to simulated and observed data.
# y is log(estimate / true value); x is log(anchor / true value).

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(lme4); library(metafor); library(data.table) })

# Gross-error rule: drop responses further from the true value (log scale) than both a factor of
# 1,000 and ten times the most extreme anchor used for that cell. A response equal to any anchor
# is always retained, so the rule cannot remove strongly anchored answers.
drop_gross_errors <- function(dat) {
  dat <- dat[is.finite(y)]
  dat[, y_limit := pmax(log(1000), max(abs(x)) + log(10)), by = cell]
  dat[abs(y) <= y_limit][, y_limit := NULL][]
}

# Within-item response function: y = a_cell + b x + g x|x|, with uncorrelated random intercepts,
# slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by participant. b is the average elasticity at the true value; g > 0 means the
# local elasticity rises with anchor extremity, g < 0 means it falls.
fit_within <- function(dat) {
  dat <- drop_gross_errors(dat)
  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  m <- lmer(y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid), data = dat,
            control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE, check.conv.singular = "ignore"))
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  b <- co["x", "Estimate"]; g <- co["xx", "Estimate"]
  V <- as.matrix(vcov(m))[c("x", "xx"), c("x", "xx")]
  # Relative curvature rho = g / b, with a delta-method standard error.
  grad <- c(-g / b^2, 1 / b)
  list(model = m, b = b, b_se = co["x", "Std. Error"], g = g, g_se = co["xx", "Std. Error"],
       rho = g / b, rho_se = sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% V %*% grad)), n = nrow(dat))
}

# Across-cell anchoring index: log-scale index per two-anchor cell, meta-regressed on extremity
# (mean absolute log distance of the two anchors from the true value).
cell_indices <- function(rows, cells) {
  r <- merge(drop_gross_errors(rows)[, .(cell, anchorhigh, y)], cells[, .(cell, study, x_low, x_high, extremity)], by = "cell")
  r[, .(med_high = median(y[anchorhigh == 1]), med_low = median(y[anchorhigh == 0]),
        mad_high = mad(y[anchorhigh == 1]), mad_low = mad(y[anchorhigh == 0]),
        n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1), n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0),
        study = study[1], x_low = x_low[1], x_high = x_high[1], extremity = extremity[1]), by = cell][
    , `:=`(ai = (med_high - med_low) / (x_high - x_low),
           ai_se = 1.2533 * sqrt(pmax(mad_high, 1e-3)^2 / n_high + pmax(mad_low, 1e-3)^2 / n_low) / (x_high - x_low))][]
}

fit_across <- function(ci) {
  m <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci, method = "REML")
  list(model = m, slope = unname(coef(m)["extremity"]), slope_se = unname(m$se[2]),
       intercept = unname(coef(m)["intrcpt"]), mean_ai = weighted.mean(ci$ai, 1 / ci$ai_se^2))
}

PART 1
# Confirmatory analyses as preregistered (prereg/preregistration.md, Q19-Q24).
# Usage: Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R          -> observed OpAQ estimates (after the prereg commit)
#        Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R dry-run  -> estimates replaced by responses simulated from M2,
#                                               to check the pipeline without reading outcomes

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(quantreg) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))

dry_run <- identical(commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE), "dry-run")
out_dir <- if (dry_run) file.path("output", "dry_run") else file.path("output", "confirmatory")
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
rho_bounds <- c(-0.05, 0.05)
slope_bounds <- c(-0.03, 0.03)

# ---- Data -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = !dry_run))
if (dry_run) {
  set.seed(1)
  cells <- unique(c(sets$within$cell, sets$across_rows$cell))
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), 0, 0.3))
  for (nm in c("within", "across_rows")) {
    s <- sets[[nm]]
    s[, estimate := t * exp(simulate_responses("M2", s[, .(cell, pid, x)], cellpar, list(w = 0.45)))]
  }
}
add_y <- function(d) {
  d <- copy(d)
  d[, est := suppressWarnings(as.numeric(estimate))]
  d[, y := fifelse(!is.na(est) & est > 0, log(est / t), NA_real_)]
  d
}
W <- add_y(sets$within)
A <- add_y(sets$across_rows)
cells_A <- copy(sets$across_cells)
exclusions <- rbind(
  data.table(set = "within", rows = nrow(W), invalid_estimate = W[is.na(y), .N],
             gross_error = nrow(W[!is.na(y)]) - nrow(drop_gross_errors(W[!is.na(y)]))),
  data.table(set = "across", rows = nrow(A), invalid_estimate = A[is.na(y), .N],
             gross_error = nrow(A[!is.na(y)]) - nrow(drop_gross_errors(A[!is.na(y)]))))
W <- W[!is.na(y)]
A <- A[!is.na(y)]

# Re-check cell eligibility after exclusions (Q14).
W_ok <- drop_gross_errors(W)[, .(levels = uniqueN(a)), by = cell][levels >= min_levels_within, cell]
W <- W[cell %in% W_ok]
A_ok <- drop_gross_errors(A)[, .(n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0), n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1)), by = cell][
  n_low >= min_n_side & n_high >= min_n_side, cell]
A <- A[cell %in% A_ok]
cells_A <- cells_A[cell %in% A_ok]

# ---- H1: within-item response function ----------------------------------------------------------
fit_h1 <- function(dat, formula = y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid)) {
  dat <- drop_gross_errors(dat)
  dat[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  # Q23: simplify random effects step by step if the fit is singular or fails to converge
  forms <- list(formula,
                update(formula, . ~ . - (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 + x || cell)),
                update(formula, . ~ . - (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | cell)))
  for (i in seq_along(forms)) {
    m <- tryCatch(lmerTest::lmer(forms[[i]], data = dat, REML = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(m) && !isSingular(m) && length(m@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages) == 0) break
  }
  co <- summary(m, ddf = "Satterthwaite")$coefficients
  V <- as.matrix(vcov(m))[c("x", "xx"), c("x", "xx")]
  b <- co["x", "Estimate"]; g <- co["xx", "Estimate"]
  grad <- c(-g / b^2, 1 / b)
  rho_se <- sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% V %*% grad))
  ci <- function(term) co[term, "Estimate"] + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, co[term, "df"]) * co[term, "Std. Error"]
  list(model = m, random_structure = i, n_rows = nrow(dat), n_cells = uniqueN(dat$cell), n_participants = uniqueN(dat$pid),
       b = b, b_ci = ci("x"), g = g, g_ci = ci("xx"), g_df = co["xx", "df"], g_p = co["xx", "Pr(>|t|)"],
       rho = g / b, rho_ci = g / b + c(-1, 1) * z * rho_se)
}
shape_verdict <- function(gate_lo, lo, hi, rel_lo, rel_hi, bounds) {
  if (gate_lo <= 0) return("gate failed: no measurable anchoring, shape not testable")
  if (rel_lo > bounds[1] && rel_hi < bounds[2]) return("flat")
  if (lo > 0) return("rising")
  if (hi < 0) return("falling")
  "inconclusive"
}
h1 <- list(pooled = fit_h1(W), random = fit_h1(W[anchortype == 1]), fixed = fit_h1(W[anchortype != 1]))
h1_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(h1), function(k) with(h1[[k]], data.table(
  set = k, n_rows, n_cells, n_participants, random_structure,
  b, b_lo = b_ci[1], b_hi = b_ci[2], g, g_lo = g_ci[1], g_hi = g_ci[2], g_df, g_p,
  rho, rho_lo = rho_ci[1], rho_hi = rho_ci[2],
  verdict = shape_verdict(b_ci[1], g_ci[1], g_ci[2], rho_ci[1], rho_ci[2], rho_bounds)))))

# ---- H2: across-cell anchoring index -------------------------------------------------------------
ci_A <- cell_indices(A, cells_A)
fit_h2 <- function(ci, mods = ~ extremity) {
  m <- tryCatch(rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = mods, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci, method = "REML"),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  robust_fallback <- is.null(m)
  if (robust_fallback) {   # Q23 fallback
    m <- robust(rma(ai, ai_se^2, mods = mods, data = ci, method = "REML"), cluster = ci$study,
                clubSandwich = requireNamespace("clubSandwich", quietly = TRUE))
  }
  list(model = m, robust_fallback = robust_fallback)
}
h2_mean <- fit_h2(ci_A, mods = ~ 1)$model
h2 <- fit_h2(ci_A)
h2_coef <- function(m, term = "extremity") {
  i <- which(rownames(m$beta) == term)
  c(est = m$beta[i], lo = m$ci.lb[i], hi = m$ci.ub[i], p = m$pval[i])
}
s2 <- h2_coef(h2$model)
h2_tab <- data.table(n_cells = nrow(ci_A), n_studies = uniqueN(ci_A$study), n_rows = nrow(drop_gross_errors(A)),
                     mean_ai = h2_mean$beta[1], mean_ai_lo = h2_mean$ci.lb, mean_ai_hi = h2_mean$ci.ub,
                     slope = s2[["est"]], slope_lo = s2[["lo"]], slope_hi = s2[["hi"]], slope_p = s2[["p"]],
                     robust_fallback = h2$robust_fallback)
h2_tab[, verdict := shape_verdict(mean_ai_lo, slope_lo, slope_hi, slope_lo, slope_hi, slope_bounds)]

# ---- H3: model adequacy ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
pi <- fread(file.path("output", "predictive_intervals.csv"))
obs <- list(g = h1$pooled$g, rho = h1$pooled$rho, slope = h2_tab$slope,
            # same estimator as fit_across() in the simulation (deviation D1 in deviations.md)
            mean_ai_weighted = weighted.mean(ci_A$ai, 1 / ci_A$ai_se^2))
h3_tab <- pi[, .(model,
                 g_inside = obs$g >= g_lo & obs$g <= g_hi,
                 rho_inside = obs$rho >= rho_lo & obs$rho <= rho_hi,
                 slope_inside = obs$slope >= slope_lo & obs$slope <= slope_hi,
                 b_inside = h1$pooled$b >= b_lo & h1$pooled$b <= b_hi,
                 mean_ai_inside = obs$mean_ai_weighted >= ai_lo & obs$mean_ai_weighted <= ai_hi,
                 mean_ai_weighted = obs$mean_ai_weighted)]
# Shape criteria decide survival; level criteria (b, mean index) depend on the calibration to
# Jacowitz & Kahneman and are reported separately. M0 is also contradicted when gate G1 passes.
h3_tab[, survives_shape := (g_inside | rho_inside) & slope_inside]
h3_tab[model == "M0", survives_shape := survives_shape & h1$pooled$b_ci[1] <= 0]
h3_tab[, survives_level := b_inside & mean_ai_inside]

# ---- Robustness (Q24) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
rob <- list()
# R1: median regression without the gross-error rule, participant-cluster bootstrap
{
  d <- copy(W)[, xx := x * abs(x)]
  f <- y ~ 0 + factor(cell) + factor(cell):x + xx
  est <- coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = d))["xx"]
  pids <- unique(d$pid)
  set.seed(20260927)
  boot <- replicate(if (dry_run) 100 else 1000, {
    s <- data.table(pid = sample(pids, replace = TRUE))[, draw := .I]
    bd <- d[s, on = "pid", allow.cartesian = TRUE]
    tryCatch(coef(rq(f, tau = 0.5, data = bd))["xx"], error = function(e) NA_real_)
  })
  rob$R1_median_regression_g <- c(est = unname(est), lo = unname(quantile(boot, .025, na.rm = TRUE)), hi = unname(quantile(boot, .975, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
# R2: piecewise slopes, knot at |x| = 1
{
  d <- drop_gross_errors(W)[, h := sign(x) * pmax(abs(x) - 1, 0)]
  m <- withCallingHandlers(lmerTest::lmer(y ~ x + h + (1 + x + h || cell) + (1 | pid), data = d),
                           warning = function(w) { message("R2 warning: ", conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  rob$R2_far_minus_near_slope <- c(est = co["h", "Estimate"], lo = co["h", "Estimate"] - qt(.975, co["h", "df"]) * co["h", "Std. Error"],
                                   hi = co["h", "Estimate"] + qt(.975, co["h", "df"]) * co["h", "Std. Error"])
}
# R3: without Bahník (2021a)
{
  f3 <- withCallingHandlers(fit_h1(W[reference_short != "Bahník, 2021a"]),
                            warning = function(w) { message("R3 warning: ", conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
  rob$R3_without_bahnik_g <- c(est = f3$g, lo = f3$g_ci[1], hi = f3$g_ci[2])
}
# R4: raw-scale anchoring index
{
  r <- merge(drop_gross_errors(A)[, .(cell, anchorhigh, est)], cells_A[, .(cell, study, a_low, a_high, extremity)], by = "cell")
  ci4 <- r[, .(ai = (median(est[anchorhigh == 1]) - median(est[anchorhigh == 0])) / (a_high[1] - a_low[1]),
               ai_se = 1.2533 * sqrt(mad(est[anchorhigh == 1])^2 / sum(anchorhigh == 1) + mad(est[anchorhigh == 0])^2 / sum(anchorhigh == 0)) / (a_high[1] - a_low[1]),
               study = study[1], extremity = extremity[1]), by = cell][ai_se > 0]
  rob$R4_raw_index_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci4)$model)
}
# R5: covariates
{
  cov <- unique(sets$across_rows[, .(cell, anchortype = factor(anchortype), comparative_question, direction,
                                     incentive_any = as.integer(incentive != 0), experiment_type = factor(experiment_type))], by = "cell")
  ci5 <- merge(ci_A, cov, by = "cell")
  keep <- names(which(sapply(ci5[, .(anchortype, comparative_question, direction, incentive_any, experiment_type)], uniqueN) > 1))
  rob$R5_covariates_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci5, mods = reformulate(c("extremity", keep)))$model)
}
# R6: without Weber et al. (2021)
rob$R6_without_weber_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci_A[study != "Weber et al., 2021"])$model)
# R7: alternative extremity measures
{
  ci7 <- copy(ci_A)[, `:=`(ext_max = pmax(abs(x_low), abs(x_high)), ext_spread = x_high - x_low)]
  rob$R7_max_distance_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci7, mods = ~ ext_max)$model, "ext_max")
  rob$R7_log_spread_slope <- h2_coef(fit_h2(ci7, mods = ~ ext_spread)$model, "ext_spread")
}
rob_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(rob), function(k) data.table(analysis = k, est = rob[[k]][1], lo = rob[[k]][2], hi = rob[[k]][3])))

# ---- Save ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
fwrite(exclusions, file.path(out_dir, "exclusions.csv"))
fwrite(h1_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h1_within.csv"))
fwrite(h2_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h2_across.csv"))
fwrite(ci_A, file.path(out_dir, "h2_cell_indices.csv"))
fwrite(h3_tab, file.path(out_dir, "h3_model_adequacy.csv"))
fwrite(rob_tab, file.path(out_dir, "robustness.csv"))
saveRDS(list(h1 = h1, h2 = h2, h2_mean = h2_mean, W = W, A = A, ci_A = ci_A), file.path(out_dir, "fits.rds"))
print(exclusions); print(h1_tab); print(h2_tab); print(h3_tab); print(rob_tab)

PART 2
# Generative process models of anchored estimation on the log scale.
# All quantities are log(value / true value); sigma is the item's belief uncertainty,
# and every model parameter is expressed in units of sigma, so the models are scale-free.
#
# Each participant-item row has a belief centre mu = bias + person offset + belief noise.
# Response = model output + response noise; a small share of responses is contaminated
# (unit errors, typing slips) to mimic real estimation data.

belief_sd_share <- 0.6     # SD of belief centres across people, in sigma units
response_sd_share <- 0.3   # response noise SD, in sigma units
contamination_p <- 0.02    # share of responses with gross errors
contamination_sd <- 2      # SD (log units) of gross errors

model_names <- c(M0 = "No anchoring", M1 = "Anchor-and-adjust, fixed number of adjustments",
                 M1R = "Resource-rational anchor-and-adjust (adaptive number of adjustments)",
                 M2 = "Constant-weight integration", M3 = "Adjust to plausible boundary",
                 M4 = "Plausibility-discounted integration")

# Metropolis-Hastings adjustment from the anchor towards the belief N(mu, sigma^2)
# (Lieder et al., 2018a). steps can differ by row; proposals have SD s * sigma.
adjust <- function(x, mu, sigma, s, steps) {
  z <- x
  for (i in seq_len(max(steps))) {
    active <- steps >= i
    prop <- z + rnorm(length(z), 0, s * sigma)
    log_ratio <- ((z - mu)^2 - (prop - mu)^2) / (2 * sigma^2)
    z <- ifelse(active & log(runif(length(z))) < log_ratio, prop, z)
  }
  z
}

# Resource-rational number of adjustments: t* minimises the expected absolute error under the
# agent's own belief plus a time cost c per adjustment (Lieder et al., 2018a, Eq. 2). The expected
# error after t steps from a standardised start distance z is tabulated once per step size s.
rr_z_grid <- seq(0, 12, by = 0.1)
rr_max_t <- 300
rr_error_curves <- local({
  cache <- list()
  function(s) {
    key <- as.character(s)
    if (is.null(cache[[key]])) {
      n <- 3000
      err <- matrix(NA_real_, length(rr_z_grid), rr_max_t + 1)
      abs_err <- function(y) 2 * dnorm(y) + y * (2 * pnorm(y) - 1)   # E|y - X|, X ~ N(0, 1)
      # Fixed seed that restores the caller's random-number state afterwards
      withr::with_seed(424242, for (j in seq_along(rr_z_grid)) {
        z <- rep(rr_z_grid[j], n)
        err[j, 1] <- mean(abs_err(z))
        for (t in seq_len(rr_max_t)) {
          prop <- z + rnorm(n, 0, s)
          z <- ifelse(log(runif(n)) < (z^2 - prop^2) / 2, prop, z)
          err[j, t + 1] <- mean(abs_err(z))
        }
      })
      cache[[key]] <<- err
    }
    cache[[key]]
  }
})
rr_steps <- function(dist_sd, s, cost) {
  err <- rr_error_curves(s)
  t_star <- apply(err, 1, function(e) which.min(e + cost * (seq_along(e) - 1)) - 1)
  t_star[pmin(round(dist_sd / 0.1) + 1, length(rr_z_grid))]
}

respond <- function(model, x, mu, sigma, par) {
  d <- x - mu
  switch(model,
    M0 = mu,
    M2 = mu + par$w * d,
    M3 = ifelse(abs(d) < par$k * sigma, x, mu + sign(d) * par$k * sigma),
    M4 = mu + par$w * d * exp(-d^2 / (2 * (par$c * sigma)^2)),
    M1 = adjust(x, mu, sigma, par$s, rep(par$t, length(x))),
    M1R = {
      # kappa: the agent's own uncertainty relative to the spread of beliefs across people
      sig <- par$kappa * sigma
      adjust(x, mu, sig, par$s, rr_steps(abs(d) / sig, par$s, par$cost))
    })
}

# rows: data.table with x (log anchor / truth), cell, pid. cellpar: data.table with cell, bias, sigma.
simulate_responses <- function(model, rows, cellpar, par, person_sd = 0.15) {
  r <- merge(rows[, .(row_id = .I, cell, pid, x)], cellpar, by = "cell")
  setorder(r, row_id)
  persons <- unique(r$pid)
  u <- setNames(rnorm(length(persons), 0, person_sd), persons)
  mu <- r$bias + u[r$pid] + rnorm(nrow(r), 0, belief_sd_share * r$sigma)
  y <- respond(model, r$x, mu, r$sigma, par) + rnorm(nrow(r), 0, response_sd_share * r$sigma)
  gross <- runif(nrow(r)) < contamination_p
  y[gross] <- y[gross] + rnorm(sum(gross), 0, contamination_sd)
  y
}

# Anchoring index of each model in the Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) design: anchors at the
# 15th and 85th percentiles of the unanchored response distribution.
jk_index <- function(model, par, n = 20000) {
  sd_unanchored <- sqrt(belief_sd_share^2 + response_sd_share^2)
  a <- qnorm(0.85) * sd_unanchored
  y_of <- function(x) {
    mu <- rnorm(n, 0, belief_sd_share)
    respond(model, rep(x, n), mu, 1, par) + rnorm(n, 0, response_sd_share)
  }
  (median(y_of(a)) - median(y_of(-a))) / (2 * a)
}

PART 3
# Post-hoc sensitivity analyses added after the code review (not preregistered; see deviations.md).
# S1 recalibrate the models to Jacowitz & Kahneman's raw-scale index and regenerate predictions;
# S2 study dependence of H1 (leave-one-study-out; study random effects);
# S3 influence and dependence checks for H2 (leave-one-study-out; study-clustered robust CI;
#    without the ten cells with the largest weights).

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(lmerTest); library(metafor); library(parallel) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
out_dir <- file.path("output", "sensitivity")
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
fits <- readRDS(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "fits.rds"))
res <- list()
row <- function(est, lo, hi) c(est = unname(est), lo = unname(lo), hi = unname(hi))

# ---- S1: raw-scale calibration ---------------------------------------------------------------
# The raw-scale index depends on the item's log uncertainty sigma, so it is averaged over the
# same sigma range the prediction simulation uses.
jk_index_raw <- function(model, par, n = 20000, sigmas = c(0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2)) {
  sd_unanchored <- sqrt(belief_sd_share^2 + response_sd_share^2)
  mean(sapply(sigmas, function(sg) {
    a <- qnorm(0.85) * sd_unanchored * sg
    y_of <- function(x) {
      mu <- rnorm(n, 0, belief_sd_share * sg)
      exp(respond(model, rep(x, n), mu, sg, par) + rnorm(n, 0, response_sd_share * sg))
    }
    (median(y_of(a)) - median(y_of(-a))) / (exp(a) - exp(-a))
  }))
}
set.seed(20260928)
grid <- fread(file.path("output", "calibration_grid.csv"))[model != "M0"]
invisible(lapply(unique(na.omit(grid$s)), rr_error_curves))
grid[, jk_raw := unlist(mclapply(seq_len(.N), function(i) {
  set.seed(i)
  p <- as.list(grid[i, intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c"), names(grid)), with = FALSE])
  jk_index_raw(grid$model[i], p[!sapply(p, is.na)])
}, mc.cores = 8))]
grid[, accepted_raw := jk_raw >= 0.30 & jk_raw <= 0.60]
fwrite(grid, file.path(out_dir, "S1_calibration_raw.csv"))
res$S1_accepted_points <- grid[, .(log_scale = sum(accepted), raw_scale = sum(accepted_raw), both = sum(accepted & accepted_raw)), by = model]

sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
within_rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x, anchortype)]
across_rows <- sets$across_rows[, .(cell, pid, x, anchorhigh)]
cells <- unique(c(within_rows$cell, across_rows$cell))
acc <- grid[accepted_raw == TRUE]
jobs <- CJ(model = unique(acc$model), rep = 1:200)
pred <- rbindlist(mclapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
  set.seed(9e5 + i)
  mdl <- jobs$model[i]
  g <- acc[acc$model == mdl]
  keep <- names(which(sapply(g, function(v) !all(is.na(v)))))
  par <- as.list(g[sample(.N, 1), intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c"), keep), with = FALSE])
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), 0.3, 1.2), bias = rnorm(length(cells), runif(1, -0.3, 0.3), 0.3))
  w <- copy(within_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(mdl, within_rows, cellpar, par)]
  a <- copy(across_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(mdl, across_rows, cellpar, par)]
  fw <- tryCatch(fit_within(w), error = function(e) NULL)
  fa <- tryCatch(fit_across(cell_indices(a, sets$across_cells)), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(fw) || is.null(fa)) return(NULL)
  data.table(model = mdl, b = fw$b, g = fw$g, rho = fw$rho, d = fa$slope, mean_ai = fa$mean_ai)
}, mc.cores = 8))
q <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", median(v), quantile(v, .025), quantile(v, .975))
s1_pi <- pred[, .(reps = .N, b = q(b), g = q(g), rho = q(rho), d = q(d), mean_ai = q(mean_ai),
                  g_lo = quantile(g, .025), g_hi = quantile(g, .975), rho_lo = quantile(rho, .025), rho_hi = quantile(rho, .975),
                  d_lo = quantile(d, .025), d_hi = quantile(d, .975)), by = model]
h1p <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h1_within.csv"))[set == "pooled"]
h2 <- fread(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "h2_across.csv"))
s1_pi[, survives_shape := ((h1p$g >= g_lo & h1p$g <= g_hi) | (h1p$rho >= rho_lo & h1p$rho <= rho_hi)) & h2$slope >= d_lo & h2$slope <= d_hi]
fwrite(s1_pi, file.path(out_dir, "S1_predictions_raw_calibration.csv"))

# ---- S2: study dependence of H1 -------------------------------------------------------------
W <- drop_gross_errors(fits$W)[, xx := x * abs(x)]
fit_g <- function(d, f = y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid)) {
  m <- suppressWarnings(lmerTest::lmer(f, data = d))
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  row(co["xx", 1], co["xx", 1] - qt(.975, co["xx", "df"]) * co["xx", 2], co["xx", 1] + qt(.975, co["xx", "df"]) * co["xx", 2])
}
for (s in unique(W$reference_short)) res[[paste0("S2_without_", s)]] <- fit_g(W[reference_short != s])
res$S2_study_random_effect <- fit_g(W, y ~ x + xx + (1 + x + xx || reference_short) + (1 + x + xx || cell) + (1 | pid))
res$S2_bahnik_only <- fit_g(W[reference_short == "Bahník, 2021a"])
res$S2_imhoff_barker_only <- {
  d <- W[reference_short == "Imhoff & Barker, 2022, Study 2"]
  co <- summary(lm(y ~ x + xx, data = d))$coefficients
  row(co["xx", 1], co["xx", 1] - qt(.975, nrow(d) - 3) * co["xx", 2], co["xx", 1] + qt(.975, nrow(d) - 3) * co["xx", 2])
}

# ---- S3: H2 influence and dependence ----------------------------------------------------------
ci_A <- fits$ci_A
h2m <- fits$h2$model
rob <- robust(h2m, cluster = ci_A$study, clubSandwich = TRUE)
res$S3_cluster_robust_slope <- row(rob$beta[2], rob$ci.lb[2], rob$ci.ub[2])
wt <- ci_A[, w := 1 / ai_se^2][order(-w)]
top10 <- wt$cell[1:10]
m10 <- rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci_A[!cell %in% top10])
res$S3_without_top10_weight_cells <- row(m10$beta[2], m10$ci.lb[2], m10$ci.ub[2])
loo <- rbindlist(lapply(unique(ci_A$study), function(s) {
  m <- tryCatch(rma.mv(ai, ai_se^2, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = ci_A[study != s]), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  data.table(study = s, slope = m$beta[2], lo = m$ci.lb[2], hi = m$ci.ub[2])
}))
fwrite(loo, file.path(out_dir, "S3_leave_one_study_out.csv"))
res$S3_loo_slope_range <- row(median(loo$slope), min(loo$slope), max(loo$slope))
res$S3_top10_weight_share <- row(sum(wt$w[1:10]) / sum(wt$w), NA, NA)

tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res)[names(res) != "S1_accepted_points"], function(k)
  data.table(analysis = k, est = res[[k]][1], lo = res[[k]][2], hi = res[[k]][3])))
fwrite(tab, file.path(out_dir, "sensitivity_results.csv"))
fwrite(res$S1_accepted_points, file.path(out_dir, "S1_accepted_points.csv"))
print(res$S1_accepted_points); print(s1_pi[, .(model, reps, b, g, rho, d, mean_ai, survives_shape)]); print(tab); print(loo)

# Inclusion rules shared by the prediction simulation and the confirmatory analysis.
# build_sets() works on design columns; when `estimate` is present it is carried along.

source(file.path("R", "read_opaq.R"))

ratio_tasktypes <- c("quantity", "number", "price", "length", "height", "distance",
                     "weight", "population", "volume", "speed", "duration", "birth rate",
                     "income", "width", "area", "circumference", "age")
# Studies whose anchors were computed from each participant's own unanchored estimates.
endogenous_anchor_studies <- c("Röseler & Wagner, 2021")

min_levels_within <- 3     # distinct anchor values per cell for the within-item set
min_log_spread <- 0.25     # across-cell set: log(A_high / A_low) of at least 0.25
min_n_side <- 10           # across-cell set: at least 10 estimates per anchor side

build_sets <- function(d) {
  d <- copy(d)
  d[, `:=`(a = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(anchor)), t = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(true_value)))]
  d[, cell := paste(reference_short, anchoring_item, sep = " || ")]
  d[, pid := paste(reference_short, participant_id, sep = " || ")]
  base <- d[anchortype %in% 1:3 & scaletype == 1 & tasktype %in% ratio_tasktypes &
              !is.na(a) & a > 0 & !is.na(t) & t > 0 &
              !reference_short %in% endogenous_anchor_studies]
  base[, t := t[1], by = cell]   # one true value per cell
  base[, x := log(a / t)]        # anchor position relative to truth (log scale)

  lev <- base[, .(n_levels = uniqueN(a), anchortype = min(anchortype)), by = cell]
  within <- base[cell %in% lev[n_levels >= min_levels_within, cell]]

  pairs <- base[anchortype %in% 2:3 & !is.na(anchorhigh)]
  pc <- pairs[, .(study = reference_short[1], item = anchoring_item[1], t = t[1],
                  n_low_values = uniqueN(a[anchorhigh == 0]), n_high_values = uniqueN(a[anchorhigh == 1]),
                  a_low = a[anchorhigh == 0][1], a_high = a[anchorhigh == 1][1],
                  n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0), n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1),
                  anchortype = anchortype[1]), by = cell]
  pc <- pc[n_low_values == 1 & n_high_values == 1 & a_high > a_low &
             log(a_high / a_low) >= min_log_spread & n_low >= min_n_side & n_high >= min_n_side]
  pc[, `:=`(x_low = log(a_low / t), x_high = log(a_high / t))]
  pc[, extremity := (abs(x_low) + abs(x_high)) / 2]
  across <- pairs[cell %in% pc$cell]

  list(within = within, across_rows = across, across_cells = pc)
}

# Inclusion rules shared by the prediction simulation and the confirmatory analysis.
# build_sets() works on design columns; when `estimate` is present it is carried along.

source(file.path("R", "read_opaq.R"))

ratio_tasktypes <- c("quantity", "number", "price", "length", "height", "distance",
                     "weight", "population", "volume", "speed", "duration", "birth rate",
                     "income", "width", "area", "circumference", "age")
# Studies whose anchors were computed from each participant's own unanchored estimates.
endogenous_anchor_studies <- c("Röseler & Wagner, 2021")

min_levels_within <- 3     # distinct anchor values per cell for the within-item set
min_log_spread <- 0.25     # across-cell set: log(A_high / A_low) of at least 0.25
min_n_side <- 10           # across-cell set: at least 10 estimates per anchor side

build_sets <- function(d) {
  d <- copy(d)
  d[, `:=`(a = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(anchor)), t = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(true_value)))]
  d[, cell := paste(reference_short, anchoring_item, sep = " || ")]
  d[, pid := paste(reference_short, participant_id, sep = " || ")]
  base <- d[anchortype %in% 1:3 & scaletype == 1 & tasktype %in% ratio_tasktypes &
              !is.na(a) & a > 0 & !is.na(t) & t > 0 &
              !reference_short %in% endogenous_anchor_studies]
  base[, t := t[1], by = cell]   # one true value per cell
  base[, x := log(a / t)]        # anchor position relative to truth (log scale)

  lev <- base[, .(n_levels = uniqueN(a), anchortype = min(anchortype)), by = cell]
  within <- base[cell %in% lev[n_levels >= min_levels_within, cell]]

  pairs <- base[anchortype %in% 2:3 & !is.na(anchorhigh)]
  pc <- pairs[, .(study = reference_short[1], item = anchoring_item[1], t = t[1],
                  n_low_values = uniqueN(a[anchorhigh == 0]), n_high_values = uniqueN(a[anchorhigh == 1]),
                  a_low = a[anchorhigh == 0][1], a_high = a[anchorhigh == 1][1],
                  n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0), n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1),
                  anchortype = anchortype[1]), by = cell]
  pc <- pc[n_low_values == 1 & n_high_values == 1 & a_high > a_low &
             log(a_high / a_low) >= min_log_spread & n_low >= min_n_side & n_high >= min_n_side]
  pc[, `:=`(x_low = log(a_low / t), x_high = log(a_high / t))]
  pc[, extremity := (abs(x_low) + abs(x_high)) / 2]
  across <- pairs[cell %in% pc$cell]

  list(within = within, across_rows = across, across_cells = pc)
}

220 estimates, 1,492 participants). Fifteen cells used random anchors: 13 221 general-knowledge items from Bahník (2021), in which each participant 222 compared 13 random anchors between 1 and 1,000 to 13 lengths and 223 heights, and two items from Yoon et al. (2021). Five cells used fixed 224 anchors: four items with 10 high anchor levels each from unpublished 225 data by Frech et al. (2021) and one item with 20 anchor levels from 226 unpublished data by Imhoff and Barker (2022), both contributed to 227 OpAQ. 228 - **Across-cell set** (secondary): cells with fixed or relevant anchors, 229 exactly one low and one high anchor value, a log ratio of at least 230 0.25 between them, and at least 10 estimates per anchor. It contains 231 129 cells from 40 studies (24,147 estimates). 232 233 ## Measures 234 235 For every estimate we computed *y* = ln(estimate / true value) and *x* = 236 ln(anchor / true value). Working on the log scale treats a doubling of a 237 height and a doubling of a population alike and matches the roughly 238 log-normal spread of numeric estimates. The log elasticity, the change 239 in *y* per unit change in *x*, is a unitless proportional pull: an 240 elasticity of .5 means that doubling the anchor multiplies the estimate 241 by about 1.41. 242 243 In the within-item set we modelled *y* = *a*cell + *b*·*x* + 244 *g*·*x*\|*x*\|. Here *b* is the average elasticity at the true value, 245 and the curvature *g* describes how the local elasticity (*b* + 246 2*g*\|*x*\|) changes as the anchor moves away from the true value in 247 either direction. We also report the relative curvature ρ = *g*/*b*, 248 which does not depend on the overall strength of anchoring. In the 249 across-cell set we computed each cell’s log anchoring index, the 250 difference between the median *y* under the high and the low anchor 251 divided by the log ratio of the anchors, and each cell’s extremity, the 252 mean absolute log distance of its two anchors from the true value. 253 254 ## Model predictions 255 256 The five process models and the no-anchoring baseline were implemented 257 on the log scale 258 (Figure 1; specification 259 in `R/models.R`). Every participant-item combination had a belief centre 260 drawn around the true value, with item-level bias and between-person 261 spread. Responses included response noise and a 2% share of gross 262 errors. Model parameters are expressed in units of the item’s belief 263 uncertainty σ, which was drawn from 0.3 to 1.2 log units per item. 264 265 To fix the models’ parameters without using OpAQ outcomes, we calibrated 266 each model to the anchoring index that Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) 267 reported for anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles of unanchored 268 estimates (about .49), accepting parameter values that produced an index 269 between .30 and .60. The preregistered calibration computed this index 270 on the log scale; a raw-scale recalibration is reported as a sensitivity 271 analysis. The number of accepted grid points per model was M1: 24; M1R: 272 56; M2: 30; M3: 11; M4: 250. We then simulated each model on the exact 273 OpAQ designs (the same anchors, true values, participants and cell 274 sizes; 200 replicates for M0 and 500 for each other model), drawing 275 parameters from the accepted set, and passed each simulated dataset 276 through the estimators used for the observed data. 277 Table 1 lists the 278 resulting predictions. 279 280
281 282 Table 1: Preregistered model predictions: medians and 95% predictive 283 intervals across simulated replicates. 284 285

299 300 The predictions separate the models by shape. M1 predicts positive 301 curvature (median *g* = 0.062), M2 zero curvature, and M3 and M4 302 negative curvature (-0.046 and -0.066). M1R’s curvature depends on its 303 parameters, with a predictive interval spanning zero. The across-cell 304 slope follows the same pattern. 305 306 ## Analysis plan 307 308 **H1 (primary).** In the within-item set we fitted a linear mixed model 309 with fixed effects for *x* and *x*\|*x*\|, uncorrelated random 310 intercepts, slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by 311 participant, using lme4 and lmerTest (Bates et al., 2015; Kuznetsova et 312 al., 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2026). Confidence intervals for *b* and 313 *g* used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; the interval for ρ used a 314 delta-method standard error. Estimates were removed as gross errors when 315 their log distance from the true value exceeded both ln(1000) and the 316 cell’s largest anchor distance plus ln(10), a rule that never removes a 317 response equal to an anchor. H1a and H1b applied the same model to the 318 random-anchor and fixed-anchor strata. 319 320 **Decision rules.** The shape test was interpreted only if the 321 confidence interval for *b* lay above zero (gate G1). We then classified 322 the curvature, in this order, as *flat* if the confidence interval for ρ 323 lay within the equivalence bounds ±0.05, as *rising* if the interval for 324 *g* lay above zero, as *falling* if it lay below zero, and otherwise as 325 inconclusive. The bounds sit just below the smallest relative curvature 326 in the 95% predictive interval of M1, M3 and M4 and far outside that of 327 M2 (Lakens, 2017). Applied to the simulated replicates, this rule 328 labelled data generated by M1 as rising in more than 99% of replicates, 329 data from M3 and M4 as falling in more than 99%, data from M2 as flat in 330 more than 99%, and data from M0 as failing the gate in all replicates. 331 332 **H2 (secondary).** We regressed the cell-level log anchoring index on 333 extremity in a multilevel meta-regression with random intercepts for 334 studies and cells within studies (Viechtbauer, 2010), using standard 335 errors derived from the median absolute deviation (MAD) of each 336 condition. Gate G2 required the mean index to exceed zero; the slope *d* 337 was classified with the same ordered rule and equivalence bounds of 338 ±0.03. 339 340 **H3 (model adequacy).** A model was contradicted when the observed 341 curvature (*g* or ρ) or the across-cell slope *d* fell outside its 95% 342 predictive interval; M0 was also contradicted if gate G1 passed. The 343 observed level of anchoring (*b* and the mean index) was compared with 344 each model’s interval but did not decide survival, because levels 345 inherit the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman’s design. 346 347 **Robustness.** We preregistered seven robustness analyses: median 348 regression without the gross-error rule, with a participant-cluster 349 bootstrap (Koenker, 2026; Koenker & Bassett, 1978); separate slopes for 350 near (\|*x*\| ≤ 1) and far anchors; H1 without Bahník (2021); H2 with 351 the raw-scale anchoring index; H2 with design covariates; H2 without one 352 study flagged by a later correction; and two alternative extremity 353 measures. 354 355 ## Deviations from the preregistration 356 357 We made four changes after the confirmatory analysis had been run. 358 First, a code review found that the observed mean anchoring index in the 359 H3 level check was computed with a different estimator from the 360 simulated one; we replaced it with the same inverse-variance weighted

570	7.4 away, 0.14. The decline appeared on both sides of the true value, in
   571	every item with enough near and far anchors, and in the one fixed-anchor
   572	item with many anchor levels. Across two-anchor studies, where authors
   573	chose one anchor pair per item, the anchoring index showed no detectable
   574	decline, and its point estimate leaned the other way.
   575	
   576	## What the within-item result rules out
   577	
   578	The negative curvature contradicts two simple accounts.
   579	Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors
   580	keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps
   581	cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight
   582	integration, the simplest version of the anchor integration model,
   583	predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. The
   584	accounts that predict a decline share one feature: the anchor’s
   585	influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment
   586	that stops at the edge of the plausible range (Epley & Gilovich, 2006),
   587	for integration that discounts implausible anchors (Turner & Schley,
   588	2016; Wegener et al., 2001), and for a resource-rational agent who
   589	invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off (Lieder et al.,
   590	2018). The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in
   591	which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects (Chapman &
   592	Johnson, 1994; Mussweiler & Strack, 2001; Wegener et al., 2001) and the
   593	distance-decaying anchoring weight of Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024),
   594	now shown with open-ended quantities and anchors varied within items.
   595	
   596	The decline was smaller than M3 and M4 predicted. Their relative
   597	curvature intervals lay below the observed value, which means that far
   598	anchors still pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or
   599	a steep plausibility discount allows. A mixture in which the weight of
   600	an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The
   601	data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one.
   602	
   603	## The across-cell pattern
   604	
   605	The across-cell analysis did not reproduce the within-item decline, and
   606	no model with a single parameter set reproduced both patterns. Two
   607	explanations are plausible, and our data cannot fully separate them.
   608	First, extremity measured against the true value is not extremity
   609	measured against people’s uncertainty. Researchers may place anchors
   610	further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. An anchor
   611	ten times the true population of a city may be less implausible than an
   612	anchor twice the height of a familiar building. When we scaled extremity
   613	by the spread of estimates, the across-cell slope turned negative, as
   614	the within-item analysis and the plausibility accounts predict. Because
   615	that spread is itself affected by anchoring, this analysis is suggestive
   616	only. Second, the two sets differ in anchor type: the within-item set is
   617	mostly random anchors, and the across-cell set only fixed or relevant
   618	anchors. The models make the same shape predictions for both, but it is
   619	possible that informative anchors lose less pull with extremity than
   620	anchors people know to be random. The fixed-anchor stratum of the
   621	within-item set pointed in the same direction as the random-anchor
   622	stratum but was too small for the preregistered test, and only one
   623	fixed-anchor item had enough anchor levels to show the decline on its
   624	own.
   625	
   626	The divergence also bears on how moderator analyses of anchoring should
   627	be read. In the same cells, the standardised effect rose with extremity
   628	while the proportional index did not change detectably. Meta-analytic
   629	findings that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised
   630	effects (Röseler & Schütz, 2022) therefore say little about whether
   631	extreme anchors are more influential per unit of distance. Tests of
   632	anchoring theories need a proportional outcome and variation in
   633	extremity that the researcher controls.
   634	
   635	## Limitations
   636	
   637	The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20
   638	within-item cells, and 83% of the within-item estimates, come from
   639	Bahník (2021), in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13
   640	different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item
   641	curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be
   642	informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that
   643	dominate applied settings. The preregistered test of the fixed-anchor
   644	stratum was not informative; in an exploratory analysis, the one
   645	fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels showed the same decline, but it
   646	is a single item. A direct test of the extremity function for
   647	informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels
   648	for many items.
   649	
   650	Second, extremity was measured relative to the true value, not relative
   651	to each participant’s belief. Where people systematically over- or
   652	underestimate a quantity, the anchor’s distance from their belief
   653	differs from its distance from the truth. The simulations included
   654	item-level bias to account for this, and the curvature was negative on
   655	both sides of the true value. However, a study that elicits unanchored
   656	estimates or plausible ranges from the same participants would give a
   657	cleaner measure.
   658	
   659	Third, the models were specified on the log scale and calibrated to a
   660	single external benchmark. The shape predictions of M1, M2, M3 and M4
   661	follow from their structure and held across all calibrated parameter
   662	values, but the level predictions depend on the calibration, and the
   663	resource-rational model’s predictions depend strongly on its time cost
   664	and on how uncertain people are. That this model survived our tests
   665	reflects the width of its predictions more than a close fit. Formal
   666	tests of resource-rational anchoring need independent measures of the
   667	time cost and of people’s uncertainty.
   668	
   669	Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and harmonisation can
   670	introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in
   671	different units from its anchors and true value, and a later correction
   672	questioned the item coding of another study. Our rules removed the
   673	first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and
   674	significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open
   675	response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages,
   676	bounded scales or preferences.
   677	
   678	## Conclusion
   679	
   680	Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller
   681	share of their distance than moderate anchors. This contradicts
   682	anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight
   683	integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor’s influence is
   684	limited by its plausibility, although the decline was weaker than simple
   685	plausibility models predict. Across studies with researcher-chosen
   686	anchors, the pattern was not visible, which suggests that comparisons
   687	across items confound anchor extremity with how well people know the
   688	quantity. For anyone choosing an anchor, the within-item evidence
   689	implies diminishing returns to extremity. For researchers, it implies
   690	that the extremity function should be estimated within items and with

   652	underestimate a quantity, the anchor’s distance from their belief

# Inclusion rules shared by the prediction simulation and the confirmatory analysis.
# build_sets() works on design columns; when `estimate` is present it is carried along.

source(file.path("R", "read_opaq.R"))

ratio_tasktypes <- c("quantity", "number", "price", "length", "height", "distance",
                     "weight", "population", "volume", "speed", "duration", "birth rate",
                     "income", "width", "area", "circumference", "age")
# Studies whose anchors were computed from each participant's own unanchored estimates.
endogenous_anchor_studies <- c("Röseler & Wagner, 2021")

min_levels_within <- 3     # distinct anchor values per cell for the within-item set
min_log_spread <- 0.25     # across-cell set: log(A_high / A_low) of at least 0.25
min_n_side <- 10           # across-cell set: at least 10 estimates per anchor side

build_sets <- function(d) {
  d <- copy(d)
  d[, `:=`(a = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(anchor)), t = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(true_value)))]
  d[, cell := paste(reference_short, anchoring_item, sep = " || ")]
  d[, pid := paste(reference_short, participant_id, sep = " || ")]
  base <- d[anchortype %in% 1:3 & scaletype == 1 & tasktype %in% ratio_tasktypes &
              !is.na(a) & a > 0 & !is.na(t) & t > 0 &
              !reference_short %in% endogenous_anchor_studies]
  base[, t := t[1], by = cell]   # one true value per cell
  base[, x := log(a / t)]        # anchor position relative to truth (log scale)

  lev <- base[, .(n_levels = uniqueN(a), anchortype = min(anchortype)), by = cell]
  within <- base[cell %in% lev[n_levels >= min_levels_within, cell]]

  pairs <- base[anchortype %in% 2:3 & !is.na(anchorhigh)]
  pc <- pairs[, .(study = reference_short[1], item = anchoring_item[1], t = t[1],
                  n_low_values = uniqueN(a[anchorhigh == 0]), n_high_values = uniqueN(a[anchorhigh == 1]),
                  a_low = a[anchorhigh == 0][1], a_high = a[anchorhigh == 1][1],
                  n_low = sum(anchorhigh == 0), n_high = sum(anchorhigh == 1),
                  anchortype = anchortype[1]), by = cell]
  pc <- pc[n_low_values == 1 & n_high_values == 1 & a_high > a_low &
             log(a_high / a_low) >= min_log_spread & n_low >= min_n_side & n_high >= min_n_side]
  pc[, `:=`(x_low = log(a_low / t), x_high = log(a_high / t))]
  pc[, extremity := (abs(x_low) + abs(x_high)) / 2]
  across <- pairs[cell %in% pc$cell]

  list(within = within, across_rows = across, across_cells = pc)
}

   228	- **Across-cell set** (secondary): cells with fixed or relevant anchors,
   229	  exactly one low and one high anchor value, a log ratio of at least
   230	  0.25 between them, and at least 10 estimates per anchor. It contains
   231	  129 cells from 40 studies (24,147 estimates).
   232	
   233	## Measures
   234	
   235	For every estimate we computed *y* = ln(estimate / true value) and *x* =
   236	ln(anchor / true value). Working on the log scale treats a doubling of a
   237	height and a doubling of a population alike and matches the roughly
   238	log-normal spread of numeric estimates. The log elasticity, the change
   239	in *y* per unit change in *x*, is a unitless proportional pull: an
   240	elasticity of .5 means that doubling the anchor multiplies the estimate
   241	by about 1.41.
   242	
   243	In the within-item set we modelled *y* = *a*<sub>cell</sub> + *b*·*x* +
   244	*g*·*x*\|*x*\|. Here *b* is the average elasticity at the true value,
   245	and the curvature *g* describes how the local elasticity (*b* +
   246	2*g*\|*x*\|) changes as the anchor moves away from the true value in
   247	either direction. We also report the relative curvature ρ = *g*/*b*,
   248	which does not depend on the overall strength of anchoring. In the
   249	across-cell set we computed each cell’s log anchoring index, the
   250	difference between the median *y* under the high and the low anchor
   251	divided by the log ratio of the anchors, and each cell’s extremity, the
   252	mean absolute log distance of its two anchors from the true value.
   253	
   254	## Model predictions
   255	
   256	The five process models and the no-anchoring baseline were implemented
   257	on the log scale
   258	(<a href="#fig-models" class="quarto-xref">Figure 1</a>; specification
   259	in `R/models.R`). Every participant-item combination had a belief centre
   260	drawn around the true value, with item-level bias and between-person
   261	spread. Responses included response noise and a 2% share of gross
   262	errors. Model parameters are expressed in units of the item’s belief
   263	uncertainty σ, which was drawn from 0.3 to 1.2 log units per item.
   264	
   265	To fix the models’ parameters without using OpAQ outcomes, we calibrated
   266	each model to the anchoring index that Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995)
   267	reported for anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles of unanchored
   268	estimates (about .49), accepting parameter values that produced an index
   269	between .30 and .60. The preregistered calibration computed this index
   270	on the log scale; a raw-scale recalibration is reported as a sensitivity
   271	analysis. The number of accepted grid points per model was M1: 24; M1R:
   272	56; M2: 30; M3: 11; M4: 250. We then simulated each model on the exact
   273	OpAQ designs (the same anchors, true values, participants and cell
   274	sizes; 200 replicates for M0 and 500 for each other model), drawing
   275	parameters from the accepted set, and passed each simulated dataset
   276	through the estimators used for the observed data.
   277	<a href="#tbl-predictions" class="quarto-xref">Table 1</a> lists the
   278	resulting predictions.

   300	The predictions separate the models by shape. M1 predicts positive
   301	curvature (median *g* = 0.062), M2 zero curvature, and M3 and M4
   302	negative curvature (-0.046 and -0.066). M1R’s curvature depends on its
   303	parameters, with a predictive interval spanning zero. The across-cell
   304	slope follows the same pattern.
   305	
   306	## Analysis plan
   307	
   308	**H1 (primary).** In the within-item set we fitted a linear mixed model
   309	with fixed effects for *x* and *x*\|*x*\|, uncorrelated random
   310	intercepts, slopes and curvatures by cell, and random intercepts by
   311	participant, using lme4 and lmerTest (Bates et al., 2015; Kuznetsova et
   312	al., 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2026). Confidence intervals for *b* and
   313	*g* used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; the interval for ρ used a
   314	delta-method standard error. Estimates were removed as gross errors when
   315	their log distance from the true value exceeded both ln(1000) and the
   316	cell’s largest anchor distance plus ln(10), a rule that never removes a
   317	response equal to an anchor. H1a and H1b applied the same model to the
   318	random-anchor and fixed-anchor strata.
   319	
   320	**Decision rules.** The shape test was interpreted only if the
   321	confidence interval for *b* lay above zero (gate G1). We then classified
   322	the curvature, in this order, as *flat* if the confidence interval for ρ
   323	lay within the equivalence bounds ±0.05, as *rising* if the interval for
   324	*g* lay above zero, as *falling* if it lay below zero, and otherwise as
   325	inconclusive. The bounds sit just below the smallest relative curvature
   326	in the 95% predictive interval of M1, M3 and M4 and far outside that of
   327	M2 (Lakens, 2017). Applied to the simulated replicates, this rule
   328	labelled data generated by M1 as rising in more than 99% of replicates,
   329	data from M3 and M4 as falling in more than 99%, data from M2 as flat in
   330	more than 99%, and data from M0 as failing the gate in all replicates.
   331	
   332	**H2 (secondary).** We regressed the cell-level log anchoring index on
   333	extremity in a multilevel meta-regression with random intercepts for
   334	studies and cells within studies (Viechtbauer, 2010), using standard
   335	errors derived from the median absolute deviation (MAD) of each
   336	condition. Gate G2 required the mean index to exceed zero; the slope *d*
   337	was classified with the same ordered rule and equivalence bounds of
   338	±0.03.
   339	
   340	**H3 (model adequacy).** A model was contradicted when the observed
   341	curvature (*g* or ρ) or the across-cell slope *d* fell outside its 95%
   342	predictive interval; M0 was also contradicted if gate G1 passed. The
   343	observed level of anchoring (*b* and the mean index) was compared with
   344	each model’s interval but did not decide survival, because levels
   345	inherit the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman’s design.
   346	
   347	**Robustness.** We preregistered seven robustness analyses: median
   348	regression without the gross-error rule, with a participant-cluster
   349	bootstrap (Koenker, 2026; Koenker & Bassett, 1978); separate slopes for
   350	near (\|*x*\| ≤ 1) and far anchors; H1 without Bahník (2021); H2 with
   351	the raw-scale anchoring index; H2 with design covariates; H2 without one
   352	study flagged by a later correction; and two alternative extremity
   353	measures.

   571	every item with enough near and far anchors, and in the one fixed-anchor
   572	item with many anchor levels. Across two-anchor studies, where authors
   573	chose one anchor pair per item, the anchoring index showed no detectable
   574	decline, and its point estimate leaned the other way.
   575	
   576	## What the within-item result rules out
   577	
   578	The negative curvature contradicts two simple accounts.
   579	Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors
   580	keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps
   581	cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight
   582	integration, the simplest version of the anchor integration model,
   583	predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. The
   584	accounts that predict a decline share one feature: the anchor’s
   585	influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment
   586	that stops at the edge of the plausible range (Epley & Gilovich, 2006),
   587	for integration that discounts implausible anchors (Turner & Schley,
   588	2016; Wegener et al., 2001), and for a resource-rational agent who
   589	invests more adjustments when the anchor is far off (Lieder et al.,
   590	2018). The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in
   591	which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects (Chapman &
   592	Johnson, 1994; Mussweiler & Strack, 2001; Wegener et al., 2001) and the
   593	distance-decaying anchoring weight of Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024),
   594	now shown with open-ended quantities and anchors varied within items.
   595	
   596	The decline was smaller than M3 and M4 predicted. Their relative
   597	curvature intervals lay below the observed value, which means that far
   598	anchors still pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or
   599	a steep plausibility discount allows. A mixture in which the weight of
   600	an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The
   601	data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one.
   602	
   603	## The across-cell pattern
   604	
   605	The across-cell analysis did not reproduce the within-item decline, and
   606	no model with a single parameter set reproduced both patterns. Two
   607	explanations are plausible, and our data cannot fully separate them.
   608	First, extremity measured against the true value is not extremity
   609	measured against people’s uncertainty. Researchers may place anchors
   610	further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. An anchor
   611	ten times the true population of a city may be less implausible than an
   612	anchor twice the height of a familiar building. When we scaled extremity
   613	by the spread of estimates, the across-cell slope turned negative, as
   614	the within-item analysis and the plausibility accounts predict. Because
   615	that spread is itself affected by anchoring, this analysis is suggestive
   616	only. Second, the two sets differ in anchor type: the within-item set is
   617	mostly random anchors, and the across-cell set only fixed or relevant
   618	anchors. The models make the same shape predictions for both, but it is
   619	possible that informative anchors lose less pull with extremity than
   620	anchors people know to be random. The fixed-anchor stratum of the
   621	within-item set pointed in the same direction as the random-anchor
   622	stratum but was too small for the preregistered test, and only one
   623	fixed-anchor item had enough anchor levels to show the decline on its
   624	own.
   625	
   626	The divergence also bears on how moderator analyses of anchoring should
   627	be read. In the same cells, the standardised effect rose with extremity
   628	while the proportional index did not change detectably. Meta-analytic
   629	findings that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised
   630	effects (Röseler & Schütz, 2022) therefore say little about whether
   631	extreme anchors are more influential per unit of distance. Tests of
   632	anchoring theories need a proportional outcome and variation in
   633	extremity that the researcher controls.
   634	
   635	## Limitations
   636	
   637	The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20
   638	within-item cells, and 83% of the within-item estimates, come from
   639	Bahník (2021), in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13
   640	different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item
   641	curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be
   642	informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that
   643	dominate applied settings. The preregistered test of the fixed-anchor
   644	stratum was not informative; in an exploratory analysis, the one
   645	fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels showed the same decline, but it
   646	is a single item. A direct test of the extremity function for
   647	informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels
   648	for many items.
   649	
   650	Second, extremity was measured relative to the true value, not relative
   651	to each participant’s belief. Where people systematically over- or
   652	underestimate a quantity, the anchor’s distance from their belief
   653	differs from its distance from the truth. The simulations included
   654	item-level bias to account for this, and the curvature was negative on
   655	both sides of the true value. However, a study that elicits unanchored
   656	estimates or plausible ranges from the same participants would give a
   657	cleaner measure.
   658	
   659	Third, the models were specified on the log scale and calibrated to a
   660	single external benchmark. The shape predictions of M1, M2, M3 and M4
   661	follow from their structure and held across all calibrated parameter
   662	values, but the level predictions depend on the calibration, and the
   663	resource-rational model’s predictions depend strongly on its time cost
   664	and on how uncertain people are. That this model survived our tests
   665	reflects the width of its predictions more than a close fit. Formal
   666	tests of resource-rational anchoring need independent measures of the
   667	time cost and of people’s uncertainty.
   668	
   669	Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and harmonisation can
   670	introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in
   671	different units from its anchors and true value, and a later correction
   672	questioned the item coding of another study. Our rules removed the
   673	first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and
   674	significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open
   675	response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages,
   676	bounded scales or preferences.
   677	
   678	## Conclusion
   679	
   680	Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller
   681	share of their distance than moderate anchors. This contradicts
   682	anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight
   683	integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor’s influence is

1 # Extreme anchors lose proportional pull: A preregistered, model-based test of how anchoring scales with anchor extremity in open trial-level data 2 Lukas Wallrich 3 4 **Abstract** 5 6 Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor’s 7 proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor 8 becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects 9 for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with 10 anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived 11 the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models 12 (anchor-and-adjust with a fixed or a resource-rational number of 13 adjustments, constant-weight integration, adjustment to the edge of the 14 plausible range, and plausibility-discounted integration), simulated 15 them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the 16 predictions before reading any estimates. In 20 item-study cells with at 17 least three anchor values (7,949 estimates, mostly random anchors), the 18 log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged 0.31 19 and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature -0.041, 20 95% CI \[-0.058, -0.023\]; relative curvature -0.13). This contradicts 21 anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight 22 integration. Across 128 two-anchor cells from 40 studies, the anchoring 23 index did not change detectably with extremity (slope 0.050, \[-0.013, 24 0.113\]). Only the resource-rational variant, whose predictions were 25 least constrained, survived the preregistered model checks. Proportional 26 anchor influence declines within items, whereas comparisons across items 27 with researcher-chosen anchors do not show this decline. 28 29 **Keywords:** anchoring, anchor extremity, process models, resource 30 rationality, secondary data analysis, preregistration 31 32 # Introduction 33 34 Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just 35 considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged 36 whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was 37 higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards 38 that number (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). The effect appears with 39 arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in 40 consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal 41 sentencing (Englich et al., 2006; Furnham & Boo, 2011; Northcraft & 42 Neale, 1987). A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 43 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of *g* = 0.69 44 (Röseler et al., 2022; Röseler & Schütz, 2022). 45 46 Whether an anchor’s influence depends on how extreme it is has practical 47 and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey 48 designers choose anchor values, and whether an extreme opening offer 49 buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this 50 relation. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make 51 different predictions about this question, so the shape of the relation 52 between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places 53 where they can be tested against each other. 54 55 ## Evidence on anchor extremity 56 57 Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. 58 Chapman & Johnson (1994) found that “implausibly extreme anchors had a 59 proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value” 60 in lottery valuations. Strack & Mussweiler (1997) found that implausible 61 anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. 62 When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, 63 estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible 64 high anchor (Mussweiler & Strack, 2001), and Wegener et al. (2001) found 65 that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These 66 studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of 67 items. 68 69 The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open 70 Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, Röseler & Schütz (2022) found that Hedges’ 71 *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value 72 and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce 73 smaller effects. Schley & Weingarten (2026) coded extremity as a binary 74 flag for anchors that the original authors described as extreme and 75 found no difference in effect size. Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024) 76 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and 77 crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance 78 between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance 79 across 30 percentage questions. 80 81 These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence 82 in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and 83 low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even 84 if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. 85 A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible 86 with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories 87 speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief 88 and anchor is carried into the estimate. Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) 89 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median 90 estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between 91 the anchors, and Röseler & Schütz (2022) called for such a unitless 92 measure “to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and 93 adjustment strength”. 94 95 ## Process models and their predictions 96 97 We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto 98 an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor 99 extremity and proportional pull 100 (Figure 1). 101 102 In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people 103 start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number 104 of stochastic steps. Lieder et al. (2018) formalised adjustment as a 105 Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards 106 the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a 107 bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of 108 the distance uncorrected, and the proportional pull rises with 109 extremity. Lieder et al. approximated the chain’s convergence as 110 geometric, which implies a constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4); 375 across-cell analysis included 128 cells and 22,533 estimates; 627 376 estimates were missing or non-positive and 987 were removed as gross 377 errors, 870 of them from the cell with the unit mismatch. 378 379 ## Within items, the proportional pull falls with extremity (H1) 380 381 Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the average 382 elasticity was *b* = 0.307, 95% CI \[0.249, 0.365\], so doubling the 383 anchor raised estimates by about 24% near the true value. The curvature 384 was negative, *g* = -0.041, \[-0.058, -0.023\], *t*(9.1) = -5.22, *p* \< 385 .001, with a relative curvature of ρ = -0.13, \[-0.18, -0.09\]. By the 386 preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. At the true 387 value an anchor carried about 31% of its log distance into the estimate. 388 The fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*\|*x*\| was 0.23 for anchors one 389 log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and 0.14 for anchors two 390 log units (a factor of 7.4) away, about half its value at the true 391 value. Figure 2 shows the 392 binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell. 393 394 In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = 0.265, 395 \[0.215, 0.316\], and *g* = -0.034, \[-0.044, -0.023\], again classified 396 as falling. In the fixed-anchor stratum the point estimates were similar 397 (*b* = 0.618, *g* = -0.085, \[-0.143, -0.027\]), but with only five 398 cells the confidence interval for *b* spanned \[-0.31, 1.55\], so the 399 gate failed and the shape was not testable there under the preregistered 400 rules. 401 402
403 404 ![](figures/fig2_within_item.png) 405 406 Figure 2: Observed within-item response functions. Points are median log 407 estimates in 0.5-unit bins of the log anchor (bins with at least 10 408 estimates), connected within each item. Blue curves are the fitted H1 409 model for each item (fixed plus item-level random effects), drawn over 410 the central 95% of that item’s anchors. The dashed line marks estimates 411 equal to the anchor. Axes differ between panels. 412 413
414 415 ## Across cells, the anchoring index shows no clear trend (H2) 416 417 Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index was 418 0.42, \[0.35, 0.48\]. The slope of the index on extremity was *d* = 419 0.050, \[-0.013, 0.113\]. This interval includes zero but is not narrow 420 enough to establish equivalence within ±0.03, so the result is 421 inconclusive under the preregistered rule 422 (Figure 3, panel A). The 423 point estimate is positive, the opposite sign to the within-item 424 curvature. 425 426
427 428 ![](figures/fig3_across_cells.png) 429 430 Figure 3: Across-cell relation between anchor extremity and anchor 431 influence. (A) Log anchoring index per cell with the preregistered 432 meta-regression line and 95% confidence band. (B) Hedges’ *g* per cell 433 (exploratory). Point area is proportional to precision (1/SE). The 434 standardised effect rises with extremity, while the proportional index 435 does not change detectably. 436 437
438 439 ## Model adequacy (H3) 440 441 Table 2 compares the observed 442 statistics with each model’s predictive interval. M1 predicts positive 443 curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 444 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict 445 negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but 446 they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals 447 for ρ lie below -0.14) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which 448 the data do not show. Under the preregistered survival rule, which 449 requires both the within-item curvature and the across-cell slope to 450 fall inside a model’s intervals, only M1R survived. It did so because 451 its predictive intervals were wide enough to contain positive, zero and 452 negative curvature. 453 454
455 456 Table 2: Observed statistics compared with each model’s 95% predictive 457 interval. Survival is decided by the shape criteria (curvature and 458 across-cell slope); level criteria are reported for completeness. 459 460
461 462 | Model | g \[PI\] | ρ \[PI\] | d \[PI\] | Survives (shape) | b and mean index inside (level) | 463 |:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---| 464 | M0 | out \[-0.008, 0.010\] | — | out \[-0.006, 0.005\] | no | no | 465 | M1 | out \[0.030, 0.095\] | out \[0.06, 0.34\] | in \[0.033, 0.120\] | no | no | 466 | M1R | out \[-0.029, 0.082\] | in \[-0.37, 1.39\] | in \[-0.117, 0.082\] | yes | yes | 467 | M2 | out \[-0.007, 0.007\] | out \[-0.02, 0.02\] | out \[-0.004, 0.004\] | no | no | 468 | M3 | in \[-0.071, -0.022\] | out \[-0.22, -0.15\] | out \[-0.133, -0.039\] | no | no | 469 | M4 | in \[-0.110, -0.017\] | out \[-0.30, -0.14\] | out \[-0.161, -0.049\] | no | yes | 470 471
472 473
474 475 Observed values: *g* = -0.041, ρ = -0.13, *d* = 0.050, *b* = 0.307, 476 weighted mean log anchoring index = 0.241. 477 478 ## Robustness 678 ## Conclusion 679 680 Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller 681 share of their distance than moderate anchors. This contradicts 682 anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight 683 integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor’s influence is 684 limited by its plausibility, although the decline was weaker than simple 685 plausibility models predict. Across studies with researcher-chosen 686 anchors, the pattern was not visible, which suggests that comparisons 687 across items confound anchor extremity with how well people know the 688 quantity. For anyone choosing an anchor, the within-item evidence 689 implies diminishing returns to extremity. Deviations are listed in 705 `deviations.md` and summarised above. 706 707 **Use of artificial intelligence.** This study was conceived, designed, 708 coded, analysed and written by an AI system, Claude Opus 5.5 709 (Anthropic), working autonomously in the Claude Code environment between 710 27 and 28 September 2026 under the instruction of the author, who set 711 the task (a complete, preregistered study in judgement and decision 712 making using open data) and its constraints. The AI chose the research 713 question, dataset, models and analyses, wrote all code and text, and 714 recorded its decisions in `decision_log.md`. Two other AI systems 715 reviewed the design, code and manuscript: OpenAI Codex CLI and Google 716 Gemini 3.8 Flash (via the Antigravity CLI); their comments and the 717 responses are in `review_log.md`. All references were retrieved from 718 Crossref or DataCite metadata by script. The author is accountable for 719 the content of the article. No AI system is listed as an author. 720 721 **Ethics.** The study used only openly licensed, anonymised secondary 722 data; no new data were collected, and no ethics approval was sought. 723 724 **Competing interests.** None. 725
