1 # Extreme anchors lose proportional pull: A preregistered, model-based test of how anchoring scales with anchor extremity in open trial-level data 2 Lukas Wallrich 3 4 **Abstract** 5 6 Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor’s 7 proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor 8 becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects 9 for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with 10 anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived 11 the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models 12 (anchor-and-adjust with a fixed or a resource-rational number of 13 adjustments, constant-weight integration, adjustment to the edge of the 14 plausible range, and plausibility-discounted integration), simulated 15 them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the 16 predictions before reading any estimates. In 20 item-study cells with at 17 least three anchor values (7,949 estimates, mostly random anchors), the 18 log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged 0.31 19 and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature -0.041, 20 95% CI \[-0.058, -0.023\]; relative curvature -0.13). This contradicts 21 anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight 22 integration. Across 128 two-anchor cells from 40 studies, the anchoring 23 index did not change detectably with extremity (slope 0.050, \[-0.013, 24 0.113\]). Only the resource-rational variant, whose predictions were 25 least constrained, survived the preregistered model checks. Proportional 26 anchor influence declines within items, whereas comparisons across items 27 with researcher-chosen anchors do not show this decline. 28 29 **Keywords:** anchoring, anchor extremity, process models, resource 30 rationality, secondary data analysis, preregistration 31 32 # Introduction 33 34 Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just 35 considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged 36 whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was 37 higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards 38 that number (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). The effect appears with 39 arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in 40 consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal 41 sentencing (Englich et al., 2006; Furnham & Boo, 2011; Northcraft & 42 Neale, 1987). A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 43 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of *g* = 0.69 44 (Röseler et al., 2022; Röseler & Schütz, 2022). 45 46 Whether an anchor’s influence depends on how extreme it is has practical 47 and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey 48 designers choose anchor values, and whether an extreme opening offer 49 buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this 50 relation. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make 51 different predictions about this question, so the shape of the relation 52 between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places 53 where they can be tested against each other. 54 55 ## Evidence on anchor extremity 56 57 Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. 58 Chapman & Johnson (1994) found that “implausibly extreme anchors had a 59 proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value” 60 in lottery valuations. Strack & Mussweiler (1997) found that implausible 61 anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. 62 When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, 63 estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible 64 high anchor (Mussweiler & Strack, 2001), and Wegener et al. (2001) found 65 that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These 66 studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of 67 items. 68 69 The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open 70 Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, Röseler & Schütz (2022) found that Hedges’ 71 *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value 72 and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce 73 smaller effects. Schley & Weingarten (2026) coded extremity as a binary 74 flag for anchors that the original authors described as extreme and 75 found no difference in effect size. Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024) 76 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and 77 crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance 78 between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance 79 across 30 percentage questions. 80 81 These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence 82 in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and 83 low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even 84 if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. 85 A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible 86 with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories 87 speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief 88 and anchor is carried into the estimate. Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) 89 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median 90 estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between 91 the anchors, and Röseler & Schütz (2022) called for such a unitless 92 measure “to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and 93 adjustment strength”. 94 95 ## Process models and their predictions 96 97 We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto 98 an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor 99 extremity and proportional pull 100 (Figure 1). 101 102 In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people 103 start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number 104 of stochastic steps. Lieder et al. (2018) formalised adjustment as a 105 Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards 106 the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a 107 bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of 108 the distance uncorrected, and the proportional pull rises with 109 extremity. Lieder et al. approximated the chain’s convergence as 110 geometric, which implies a constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4); 375 across-cell analysis included 128 cells and 22,533 estimates; 627 376 estimates were missing or non-positive and 987 were removed as gross 377 errors, 870 of them from the cell with the unit mismatch. 378 379 ## Within items, the proportional pull falls with extremity (H1) 380 381 Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the average 382 elasticity was *b* = 0.307, 95% CI \[0.249, 0.365\], so doubling the 383 anchor raised estimates by about 24% near the true value. The curvature 384 was negative, *g* = -0.041, \[-0.058, -0.023\], *t*(9.1) = -5.22, *p* \< 385 .001, with a relative curvature of ρ = -0.13, \[-0.18, -0.09\]. By the 386 preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. At the true 387 value an anchor carried about 31% of its log distance into the estimate. 388 The fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*\|*x*\| was 0.23 for anchors one 389 log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and 0.14 for anchors two 390 log units (a factor of 7.4) away, about half its value at the true 391 value. Figure 2 shows the 392 binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell. 393 394 In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = 0.265, 395 \[0.215, 0.316\], and *g* = -0.034, \[-0.044, -0.023\], again classified 396 as falling. Blue curves are the fitted H1 409 model for each item (fixed plus item-level random effects), drawn over 410 the central 95% of that item’s anchors. The dashed line marks estimates 411 equal to the anchor. Axes differ between panels. 412 413
414 415 ## Across cells, the anchoring index shows no clear trend (H2) 416 417 Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index was 418 0.42, \[0.35, 0.48\]. The slope of the index on extremity was *d* = 419 0.050, \[-0.013, 0.113\]. This interval includes zero but is not narrow 420 enough to establish equivalence within ±0.03, so the result is 421 inconclusive under the preregistered rule 422 (Figure 3, panel A). It did so because 451 its predictive intervals were wide enough to contain positive, zero and 452 negative curvature. 453 454

1:# Preregistration: How does anchor influence change with anchor extremity? A model-based secondary analysis of the Open Anchoring Quest
7:## Part 1: Study information
20:Notation. For each estimate, y = ln(estimate / true value) and x = ln(anchor / true value). Within item-study cells we fit y = a_cell + b·x + g·x|x| (plus random effects; Q19). b is the average elasticity at the true value; g is the curvature: g > 0 means the anchor's proportional pull grows with extremity, g < 0 means it shrinks. rho = g / b is the curvature relative to the average elasticity.
30:Predictions (derived by simulation on the exact OpAQ designs; Q20 and `output/predictions_summary.csv`):
34:- H3 (model adequacy): each model's 95% predictive interval for g, rho, and the across-cell slope, given in Q20. A model is contradicted by the data when an observed statistic lies outside its interval.
36:## Part 2: Data description
57:**Q13. Inclusion and exclusion of units.**
62:**Q14. Missing data.** Rows with a missing, non-numeric, zero or negative estimate are excluded (the log is undefined). We will report how many. If a cell loses its eligibility (fewer than 3 anchor values in the within set; fewer than 10 rows on a side in the across set), it is dropped.
64:**Q15. Outliers.** Gross errors (unit errors, typing slips) are removed with one rule applied identically to simulated and observed data (`drop_gross_errors()` in `R/estimators.R`): a response is dropped when |y| exceeds both ln(1000) and the cell's largest |x| plus ln(10). A response equal to any anchor is always retained. No other trimming. Robustness analysis R1 uses median regression without this rule.
68:## Part 3: Knowledge of data
74:- Columns read (design only, via `R/read_opaq.R`): reference_short, reference, id, participant_id, sex, age, nationality, anchoring_item, true_value, anchor, anchorhigh, anchortype, tasktype, direction, incentive, comparative_question, experiment_type, stimulitype, sampletype, scaletype, published, preregistered. Outputs seen: `output/design_inventory.txt`, `output/design_cells.csv`, and the cell and row counts in Q13.
78:## Part 4: Analyses
80:**Q19. Statistical models.** All code is in `R/estimators.R` (shared with the prediction simulation) and `R/04_confirmatory.R`, which was run before this commit in dry-run mode on responses simulated from M2 (`Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R dry-run`, output in `output/dry_run/`) to check that it executes.
87:H3. For each model, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of its simulated g, rho, b and d (Q20), compared with the observed values.
89:**Q20. Predicted effects and smallest effects of interest.** Model predictions from `R/03_simulate_predictions.R` (200 for M0 and 500 for each other model replicates per model; each replicate draws model parameters from the set calibrated to Jacowitz & Kahneman's (1995) anchoring index of about .49, allowing .30-.60, and draws item uncertainty sigma ~ U(0.3, 1.2) log units and item bias ~ N(U(-0.3, 0.3), 0.3)):
100:Cells are medians with 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across replicates, generated by `R/03c_prereg_tables.R` (`output/prereg_tables.md`, `output/predictive_intervals.csv`). The simulation estimator always fits the full random-effects structure with lme4; the confirmatory analysis uses the same formula in lmerTest with the Q23 fallback. Other fixed simulation assumptions (`R/models.R`): SD of belief centres across people 0.6 sigma; response noise 0.3 sigma; person offset SD 0.15; 2% of responses contaminated with N(0, 2) log-unit errors. M1R additionally has kappa, the agent's own uncertainty relative to the spread of beliefs across people (0.25-1; only 0.25-0.75 reproduce the benchmark). Calibration grid and accepted values: `output/calibration_grid.csv`.
106:**Q21. Power / precision.** Operating characteristics of the Q22 decision rules, computed by applying them to each simulated replicate (`R/03b_decision_properties.R`, `output/decision_properties.txt`):
119:**Q22. Inference criteria.**
122:  1. CI for rho entirely inside the equivalence bounds (Q20): no meaningful curvature. Consistent with M2; inconsistent with M1, M3, M4.
130:- H2 decision: the same ordered rule applied to d, with its own equivalence bounds (Q20).
134:**Q23. Analytic problems.** If the H1 model fails to converge or is singular, we remove random-effect terms in this order until it converges: curvature variance, slope variance; the participant intercept is kept. If rma.mv fails, we fit a single-level random-effects meta-regression with study-clustered robust SEs (clubSandwich if available, otherwise metafor::robust). Any such change is reported in `deviations.md`.
136:**Q24. Robustness.**
145:**Q25. Exploratory analyses (labelled as such in the paper).** Fitting each model's parameters to the observed data (simulation-based estimation) to compare fit; asymmetry between high and low anchors; the relation of Hedges' g to extremity in the across-cell set, for comparison with Röseler & Schütz (2022); plots of binned response functions for each within-item cell.

Within item-study cells we fit y = a_cell + b·x + g·x|x| (plus random effects; Q19). b is the average elasticity at the true value; g is the curvature: g > 0 means the anchor's proportional pull grows with extremity, g < 0 means it shrinks. rho = g / b is the curvature relative to the average elasticity.
30:Predictions (derived by simulation on the exact OpAQ designs; Q20 and `output/predictions_summary.csv`):
34:- H3 (model adequacy): each model's 95% predictive interval for g, rho, and the across-cell slope, given in Q20. A model is contradicted by the data when an observed statistic lies outside its interval.
36:## Part 2: Data description
57:**Q13. Inclusion and exclusion of units.**
62:**Q14. Missing data.** Rows with a missing, non-numeric, zero or negative estimate are excluded (the log is undefined). We will report how many. If a cell loses its eligibility (fewer than 3 anchor values in the within set; fewer than 10 rows on a side in the across set), it is dropped.
64:**Q15. Outliers.** Gross errors (unit errors, typing slips) are removed with one rule applied identically to simulated and observed data (`drop_gross_errors()` in `R/estimators.R`): a response is dropped when |y| exceeds both ln(1000) and the cell's largest |x| plus ln(10). A response equal to any anchor is always retained. No other trimming. Robustness analysis R1 uses median regression without this rule.
68:## Part 3: Knowledge of data
74:- Columns read (design only, via `R/read_opaq.R`): reference_short, reference, id, participant_id, sex, age, nationality, anchoring_item, true_value, anchor, anchorhigh, anchortype, tasktype, direction, incentive, comparative_question, experiment_type, stimulitype, sampletype, scaletype, published, preregistered. Outputs seen: `output/design_inventory.txt`, `output/design_cells.csv`, and the cell and row counts in Q13.
78:## Part 4: Analyses
80:**Q19. Statistical models.** All code is in `R/estimators.R` (shared with the prediction simulation) and `R/04_confirmatory.R`, which was run before this commit in dry-run mode on responses simulated from M2 (`Rscript R/04_confirmatory.R dry-run`, output in `output/dry_run/`) to check that it executes.
87:H3. For each model, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of its simulated g, rho, b and d (Q20), compared with the observed values.
89:**Q20. Predicted effects and smallest effects of interest.** Model predictions from `R/03_simulate_predictions.R` (200 for M0 and 500 for each other model replicates per model; each replicate draws model parameters from the set calibrated to Jacowitz & Kahneman's (1995) anchoring index of about .49, allowing .30-.60, and draws item uncertainty sigma ~ U(0.3, 1.2) log units and item bias ~ N(U(-0.3, 0.3), 0.3)):
100:Cells are medians with 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across replicates, generated by `R/03c_prereg_tables.R` (`output/prereg_tables.md`, `output/predictive_intervals.csv`). The simulation estimator always fits the full random-effects structure with lme4; the confirmatory analysis uses the same formula in lmerTest with the Q23 fallback. Other fixed simulation assumptions (`R/models.R`): SD of belief centres across people 0.6 sigma; response noise 0.3 sigma; person offset SD 0.15; 2% of responses contaminated with N(0, 2) log-unit errors. M1R additionally has kappa, the agent's own uncertainty relative to the spread of beliefs across people (0.25-1; only 0.25-0.75 reproduce the benchmark). Calibration grid and accepted values: `output/calibration_grid.csv`.
106:**Q21. Power / precision.** Operating characteristics of the Q22 decision rules, computed by applying them to each simulated replicate (`R/03b_decision_properties.R`, `output/decision_properties.txt`):
119:**Q22. Inference criteria.**
122:  1. CI for rho entirely inside the equivalence bounds (Q20): no meaningful curvature. Consistent with M2; inconsistent with M1, M3, M4.
130:- H2 decision: the same ordered rule applied to d, with its own equivalence bounds (Q20).
134:**Q23. Analytic problems.** If the H1 model fails to converge or is singular, we remove random-effect terms in this order until it converges: curvature variance, slope variance; the participant intercept is kept. If rma.mv fails, we fit a single-level random-effects meta-regression with study-clustered robust SEs (clubSandwich if available, otherwise metafor::robust). Any such change is reported in `deviations.md`.
136:**Q24. Robustness.**
145:**Q25. Exploratory analyses (labelled as such in the paper).** Fitting each model's parameters to the observed data (simulation-based estimation) to compare fit; asymmetry between high and low anchors; the relation of Hedges' g to extremity in the across-cell set, for comparison with Röseler & Schütz (2022); plots of binned response functions for each within-item cell.

PART 1 1 # Extreme anchors lose proportional pull: A preregistered, model-based test of how anchoring scales with anchor extremity in open trial-level data 2 Lukas Wallrich 3 4 **Abstract** 5 6 Anchors bias numeric estimates, but it is unclear whether an anchor’s 7 proportional influence rises, stays constant or falls as the anchor 8 becomes more extreme. Meta-analyses report larger standardised effects 9 for more distant anchors, yet a standardised mean difference rises with 10 anchor distance even when the proportional pull is constant. We derived 11 the shape of the anchor-response function from five process models 12 (anchor-and-adjust with a fixed or a resource-rational number of 13 adjustments, constant-weight integration, adjustment to the edge of the 14 plausible range, and plausibility-discounted integration), simulated 15 them on the designs of the Open Anchoring Quest, and preregistered the 16 predictions before reading any estimates. In 20 item-study cells with at 17 least three anchor values (7,949 estimates, mostly random anchors), the 18 log-scale elasticity of estimates with respect to anchors averaged 0.31 19 and fell as anchors moved away from the true value (curvature -0.041, 20 95% CI \[-0.058, -0.023\]; relative curvature -0.13). This contradicts 21 anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments and constant-weight 22 integration. Across 128 two-anchor cells from 40 studies, the anchoring 23 index did not change detectably with extremity (slope 0.050, \[-0.013, 24 0.113\]). Only the resource-rational variant, whose predictions were 25 least constrained, survived the preregistered model checks. Proportional 26 anchor influence declines within items, whereas comparisons across items 27 with researcher-chosen anchors do not show this decline. 28 29 **Keywords:** anchoring, anchor extremity, process models, resource 30 rationality, secondary data analysis, preregistration 31 32 # Introduction 33 34 Numeric judgements are drawn towards numbers people have just 35 considered. In the classic demonstration, participants who first judged 36 whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was 37 higher or lower than a random number gave estimates that moved towards 38 that number (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). The effect appears with 39 arbitrary and informative anchors, with lay people and experts, and in 40 consequential settings such as property valuation and criminal 41 sentencing (Englich et al., 2006; Furnham & Boo, 2011; Northcraft & 42 Neale, 1987). A meta-analysis of openly shared trial-level data from 90 43 anchoring studies estimated a pooled standardised effect of *g* = 0.69 44 (Röseler et al., 2022; Röseler & Schütz, 2022). 45 46 Whether an anchor’s influence depends on how extreme it is has practical 47 and theoretical weight. Practically, negotiators, litigants and survey 48 designers choose anchor values, and whether an extreme opening offer 49 buys proportionally more influence than a moderate one depends on this 50 relation. Theoretically, the leading accounts of anchoring make 51 different predictions about this question, so the shape of the relation 52 between anchor extremity and anchor influence is one of the few places 53 where they can be tested against each other. 54 55 ## Evidence on anchor extremity 56 57 Experiments that varied anchor extremity have produced mixed results. 58 Chapman & Johnson (1994) found that “implausibly extreme anchors had a 59 proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value” 60 in lottery valuations. Strack & Mussweiler (1997) found that implausible 61 anchors produced a larger raw shift in estimates than plausible ones. 62 When implausible anchors were placed far beyond the plausible range, 63 estimates under them were no higher than estimates under a plausible 64 high anchor (Mussweiler & Strack, 2001), and Wegener et al. (2001) found 65 that very extreme anchors had smaller effects than moderate ones. These 66 studies compared two to four anchor levels, mostly for a handful of 67 items. 68 69 The two recent meta-analyses reach different conclusions. Using the Open 70 Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) data, Röseler & Schütz (2022) found that Hedges’ 71 *g* increased with the relative distance between anchor and true value 72 and concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors produce 73 smaller effects. Schley & Weingarten (2026) coded extremity as a binary 74 flag for anchors that the original authors described as extreme and 75 found no difference in effect size. Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024) 76 modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and 77 crowd mean, with a weight that decays exponentially with the distance 78 between anchor and truth, and found that this weight fell with distance 79 across 30 percentage questions. 80 81 These results are hard to compare because they measure anchor influence 82 in different units. A standardised mean difference between high- and 83 low-anchor conditions rises with the distance between the anchors even 84 if every anchor pulls estimates by the same proportion of its distance. 85 A finding that *g* grows with anchor distance is therefore compatible 86 with constant, rising and falling proportional influence. The theories 87 speak to the proportional pull: how much of the distance between belief 88 and anchor is carried into the estimate. Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995) 89 captured this with the anchoring index, the difference between median 90 estimates under high and low anchors divided by the difference between 91 the anchors, and Röseler & Schütz (2022) called for such a unitless 92 measure “to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and 93 adjustment strength”. 94 95 ## Process models and their predictions 96 97 We consider five process models. Each maps an anchor and a belief onto 98 an estimate, and each implies a shape for the relation between anchor 99 extremity and proportional pull 100 (Figure 1). 101 102 In *anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of adjustments* (M1), people 103 start at the anchor and adjust towards their belief in a limited number 104 of stochastic steps. Lieder et al. (2018) formalised adjustment as a 105 Metropolis-Hastings chain that starts at the anchor and moves towards 106 the belief distribution. When the anchor is far away, each step covers a 107 bounded distance, so a fixed number of steps leaves a larger share of 108 the distance uncorrected, and the proportional pull rises with 109 extremity. Lieder et al. approximated the chain’s convergence as 110 geometric, which implies a constant proportional pull (their Eq. 4); 375 across-cell analysis included 128 cells and 22,533 estimates; 627 376 estimates were missing or non-positive and 987 were removed as gross 377 errors, 870 of them from the cell with the unit mismatch. 378 379 ## Within items, the proportional pull falls with extremity (H1) 380 381 Anchoring was clearly present in the within-item set: the average 382 elasticity was *b* = 0.307, 95% CI \[0.249, 0.365\], so doubling the 383 anchor raised estimates by about 24% near the true value. The curvature 384 was negative, *g* = -0.041, \[-0.058, -0.023\], *t*(9.1) = -5.22, *p* \< 385 .001, with a relative curvature of ρ = -0.13, \[-0.18, -0.09\]. By the 386 preregistered rule, the elasticity *falls* with extremity. At the true 387 value an anchor carried about 31% of its log distance into the estimate. 388 The fitted local elasticity *b* + 2*g*\|*x*\| was 0.23 for anchors one 389 log unit (a factor of 2.7) from the true value and 0.14 for anchors two 390 log units (a factor of 7.4) away, about half its value at the true 391 value. Figure 2 shows the 392 binned observed estimates and the fitted curves for each cell. 393 394 In the random-anchor stratum the result was the same: *b* = 0.265, 395 \[0.215, 0.316\], and *g* = -0.034, \[-0.044, -0.023\], again classified 396 as falling. In the fixed-anchor stratum the point estimates were similar 397 (*b* = 0.618, *g* = -0.085, \[-0.143, -0.027\]), but with only five 398 cells the confidence interval for *b* spanned \[-0.31, 1.55\], so the 399 gate failed and the shape was not testable there under the preregistered 400 rules. 401 402
403 404 ![](figures/fig2_within_item.png) 405 406 Figure 2: Observed within-item response functions. Points are median log 407 estimates in 0.5-unit bins of the log anchor (bins with at least 10 408 estimates), connected within each item. Blue curves are the fitted H1 409 model for each item (fixed plus item-level random effects), drawn over 410 the central 95% of that item’s anchors. The dashed line marks estimates 411 equal to the anchor. Axes differ between panels. 412 413
414 415 ## Across cells, the anchoring index shows no clear trend (H2) 416 417 Anchoring was present across cells: the mean log anchoring index was 418 0.42, \[0.35, 0.48\]. The slope of the index on extremity was *d* = 419 0.050, \[-0.013, 0.113\]. This interval includes zero but is not narrow 420 enough to establish equivalence within ±0.03, so the result is 421 inconclusive under the preregistered rule 422 (Figure 3, panel A). The 423 point estimate is positive, the opposite sign to the within-item 424 curvature. 425 426
427 428 ![](figures/fig3_across_cells.png) 429 430 Figure 3: Across-cell relation between anchor extremity and anchor 431 influence. (A) Log anchoring index per cell with the preregistered 432 meta-regression line and 95% confidence band. (B) Hedges’ *g* per cell 433 (exploratory). Point area is proportional to precision (1/SE). The 434 standardised effect rises with extremity, while the proportional index 435 does not change detectably. 436 437
438 439 ## Model adequacy (H3) 440 441 Table 2 compares the observed 442 statistics with each model’s predictive interval. M1 predicts positive 443 curvature and is contradicted by the negative observed curvature. M2 444 predicts no curvature and is contradicted as well. M3 and M4 predict 445 negative curvature and contain the observed *g* in their intervals, but 446 they predict stronger relative curvature than observed (their intervals 447 for ρ lie below -0.14) and a clearly negative across-cell slope, which 448 the data do not show. Under the preregistered survival rule, which 449 requires both the within-item curvature and the across-cell slope to 450 fall inside a model’s intervals, only M1R survived. It did so because 451 its predictive intervals were wide enough to contain positive, zero and 452 negative curvature. 453 454
455 456 Table 2: Observed statistics compared with each model’s 95% predictive 457 interval. Survival is decided by the shape criteria (curvature and 458 across-cell slope); level criteria are reported for completeness. 459 460
461 462 | Model | g \[PI\] | ρ \[PI\] | d \[PI\] | Survives (shape) | b and mean index inside (level) | 463 |:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---| 464 | M0 | out \[-0.008, 0.010\] | — | out \[-0.006, 0.005\] | no | no | 465 | M1 | out \[0.030, 0.095\] | out \[0.06, 0.34\] | in \[0.033, 0.120\] | no | no | 466 | M1R | out \[-0.029, 0.082\] | in \[-0.37, 1.39\] | in \[-0.117, 0.082\] | yes | yes | 467 | M2 | out \[-0.007, 0.007\] | out \[-0.02, 0.02\] | out \[-0.004, 0.004\] | no | no | 468 | M3 | in \[-0.071, -0.022\] | out \[-0.22, -0.15\] | out \[-0.133, -0.039\] | no | no | 469 | M4 | in \[-0.110, -0.017\] | out \[-0.30, -0.14\] | out \[-0.161, -0.049\] | no | yes | 470 471
472 473
474 475 Observed values: *g* = -0.041, ρ = -0.13, *d* = 0.050, *b* = 0.307, 476 weighted mean log anchoring index = 0.241. 477 478 ## Robustness 678 ## Conclusion 679 680 Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller 681 share of their distance than moderate anchors. This contradicts 682 anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight 683 integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor’s influence is 684 limited by its plausibility, although the decline was weaker than simple 685 plausibility models predict. Across studies with researcher-chosen 686 anchors, the pattern was not visible, which suggests that comparisons 687 across items confound anchor extremity with how well people know the 688 quantity. For anyone choosing an anchor, the within-item evidence 689 implies diminishing returns to extremity. For researchers, it implies 690 that the extremity function should be estimated within items and with 691 proportional measures. 692 693 # Declarations 694 695 **Data, code and materials.** The OpAQ data are openly available under 696 CC-BY 4.0 at https://osf.io/ygnvb (Günther et al., 2021). All code, the 697 preregistration, the frozen predictions, all outputs and the review 698 records are available in the project repository \[repository link to be 699 added before submission\]. `run_all.sh` reproduces all results from the 700 raw data. 701 702 **Preregistration.** The preregistration is `prereg/preregistration.md` 703 in the repository, committed before any estimate was read (git tag 704 `prereg-v1`, 27 September 2026). Deviations are listed in 705 `deviations.md` and summarised above. 706 707 **Use of artificial intelligence.** This study was conceived, designed, 708 coded, analysed and written by an AI system, Claude Opus 5.5 709 (Anthropic), working autonomously in the Claude Code environment between 710 27 and 28 September 2026 under the instruction of the author, who set 711 the task (a complete, preregistered study in judgement and decision 712 making using open data) and its constraints. The AI chose the research 713 question, dataset, models and analyses, wrote all code and text, and 714 recorded its decisions in `decision_log.md`. Two other AI systems 715 reviewed the design, code and manuscript: OpenAI Codex CLI and Google 716 Gemini 3.8 Flash (via the Antigravity CLI); their comments and the 717 responses are in `review_log.md`. All references were retrieved from 718 Crossref or DataCite metadata by script. The author is accountable for 719 the content of the article. No AI system is listed as an author. 720 721 **Ethics.** The study used only openly licensed, anonymised secondary 722 data; no new data were collected, and no ethics approval was sought. 723 724 **Competing interests.** None. 725

# The Anchoring-and-Adjustment Heuristic

Nicholas Epley, Thomas Gilovich

Volume 17, Issue 4 | April 2006

https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01704.x

Abstract
One way to make judgments under uncertainty is to anchor on information that comes to mind and adjust until a plausible estimate is reached. This anchoring-and-adjustment heuristic is assumed to underlie many intuitive judgments, and insufficient adjustment is commonly invoked to explain judgmental biases. However, despite extensive research on anchoring effects, evidence for adjustment-based anchoring biases has only recently been provided, and the causes of insufficient adjustment remain unclear. This research was designed to identify the origins of insufficient adjustment. The results of two sets of experiments indicate that adjustments from self-generated anchor values tend to be insufficient because they terminate once a plausible value is reached (Studies 1a and 1b) unless one is able and willing to search for a more accurate estimate (Studies 2a-2c).--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Abstract

Few experimental effects in the psychology of judgment and decision making have been studied as meticulously as the anchoring effect. Although the existing literature provides considerable insight into the psychological processes underlying anchoring effects, extant theories up to this point have only generated qualitative predictions. While these theories have been productive in advancing our understanding of the underlying anchoring process, they leave much to be desired in the interpretation of specific anchoring effects. In this article, we introduce the Anchor Integration Model (AIM) as a descriptive tool for the measurement and quantification of anchoring effects. We develop two versions the model: one suitable for assessing between-participant anchoring effects, and another for assessing individual differences in anchoring effects. We then fit each model to data from two experiments, and demonstrate the model’s utility in describing anchoring effects.

# Putting Adjustment Back in the Anchoring and Adjustment Heuristic: Differential Processing of Self-Generated and Experimenter-Provided Anchors

Nicholas Epley [email redacted] and Thomas GilovichView all authors and affiliations

Volume 12, Issue 5

https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9280.00372

## Abstract

People's estimates of uncertain quantities are commonly influenced by irrelevant values. These anchoring effects were originally explained as insufficient adjustment away from an initial anchor value. The existing literature provides little support for the postulated process of adjustment, however, and a consensus that none takes place seems to be emerging. We argue that this conclusion is premature, and we present evidence that insufficient adjustment produces anchoring effects when the anchors are self-generated. In Study 1, participants' verbal reports made reference to adjustment only from self-generated anchors. In Studies 2 and 3, participants induced to accept values by nodding their heads gave answers that were closer to an anchor (i.e., they adjusted less) than participants induced to deny values by shaking their heads—again, only when the anchor was self-generated. These results suggest it is time to reintroduce anchoring and adjustment as an explanation for some judgments under uncertainty.

## Abstract

Previous research on self-other similarity judgments has demonstrated that perceived similarity between self and other depends on the focus of comparison. Based on the Selective Accessibility model, which assumes that comparisons with similar others yield assimilation, whereas comparisons with dissimilar others yield contrast, the author hypothesized that the focus of a social comparison would influence its consequences. Specifically, comparing the standard to the self (focus of comparison other → self) should increase perceived similarity so that self-evaluations are assimilated to the standard. Comparing the self to the standard (focus of comparison self → other), however, should reduce perceived similarity so that contrast ensues. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(parallel) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))

n_reps <- c(M0 = 200, M1 = 500, M1R = 500, M2 = 500, M3 = 500, M4 = 500)
sigma_range <- c(0.3, 1.2)      # belief uncertainty per item (log units)
bias_centre_range <- c(-0.3, 0.3)
bias_sd <- 0.3

sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
within_rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x, anchortype)]
across_rows <- sets$across_rows[, .(cell, pid, x, anchorhigh)]
cells <- unique(c(within_rows$cell, across_rows$cell))
calib <- fread(file.path("output", "calibration_grid.csv"))[accepted == TRUE]

one_rep <- function(model, rep) {
  set.seed(1e5 * match(model, names(n_reps)) + rep)
  target <- model
  par <- if (model == "M0") list() else {
    g <- calib[calib$model == target]
    keep <- names(which(sapply(g, function(v) !all(is.na(v)))))
    as.list(g[sample(.N, 1), intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c"), keep), with = FALSE])
  }
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), sigma_range[1], sigma_range[2]),
                        bias = rnorm(length(cells), runif(1, bias_centre_range[1], bias_centre_range[2]), bias_sd))
  w <- copy(within_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, within_rows, cellpar, par)]
  a <- copy(across_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, across_rows, cellpar, par)]
  fw <- fit_within(w)
  fr <- fit_within(w[anchortype == 1])
  ff <- fit_within(w[anchortype != 1])
  fa <- fit_across(cell_indices(a, sets$across_cells))
  data.table(model, rep, par = paste(names(par), unlist(par), sep = "=", collapse = ";"),
             b = fw$b, b_se = fw$b_se, g = fw$g, g_se = fw$g_se, rho = fw$rho, rho_se = fw$rho_se,
             b_random = fr$b, g_random = fr$g, g_random_se = fr$g_se, rho_random = fr$rho, rho_random_se = fr$rho_se,
             b_fixed = ff$b, g_fixed = ff$g, g_fixed_se = ff$g_se, rho_fixed = ff$rho, rho_fixed_se = ff$rho_se,
             across_slope = fa$slope, across_slope_se = fa$slope_se, across_mean_ai = fa$mean_ai)
}

jobs <- rbindlist(lapply(names(n_reps), function(m) data.table(model = m, rep = seq_len(n_reps[[m]]))))
res <- rbindlist(mclapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
  tryCatch(one_rep(jobs$model[i], jobs$rep[i]), error = function(e) data.table(model = jobs$model[i], rep = jobs$rep[i], error = conditionMessage(e)))
}, mc.cores = 8), fill = TRUE)
fwrite(res, file.path("output", "predictions_raw.csv"))

q <- function(v) paste0(sprintf("%.3f", median(v, na.rm = TRUE)), " [", sprintf("%.3f", quantile(v, .025, na.rm = TRUE)), ", ", sprintf("%.3f", quantile(v, .975, na.rm = TRUE)), "]")
summ <- res[is.na(if ("error" %in% names(res)) error else NA), .(reps = .N, b = q(b), g = q(g), rho = q(rho), g_random = q(g_random), g_fixed = q(g_fixed),

# Predicted estimator outcomes for each process model on the exact OpAQ designs
# (anchor values, true values, participants and cell sizes). Reads design columns only.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(data.table); library(parallel) })
source(file.path("R", "design_sets.R"))
source(file.path("R", "models.R"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))

n_reps <- c(M0 = 200, M1 = 500, M1R = 500, M2 = 500, M3 = 500, M4 = 500)
sigma_range <- c(0.3, 1.2)      # belief uncertainty per item (log units)
bias_centre_range <- c(-0.3, 0.3)
bias_sd <- 0.3

sets <- build_sets(read_opaq(include_outcomes = FALSE))
within_rows <- sets$within[, .(cell, pid, x, anchortype)]
across_rows <- sets$across_rows[, .(cell, pid, x, anchorhigh)]
cells <- unique(c(within_rows$cell, across_rows$cell))
calib <- fread(file.path("output", "calibration_grid.csv"))[accepted == TRUE]

one_rep <- function(model, rep) {
  set.seed(1e5 * match(model, names(n_reps)) + rep)
  target <- model
  par <- if (model == "M0") list() else {
    g <- calib[calib$model == target]
    keep <- names(which(sapply(g, function(v) !all(is.na(v)))))
    as.list(g[sample(.N, 1), intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c"), keep), with = FALSE])
  }
  cellpar <- data.table(cell = cells, sigma = runif(length(cells), sigma_range[1], sigma_range[2]),
                        bias = rnorm(length(cells), runif(1, bias_centre_range[1], bias_centre_range[2]), bias_sd))
  w <- copy(within_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, within_rows, cellpar, par)]
  a <- copy(across_rows)[, y := simulate_responses(model, across_rows, cellpar, par)]
  fw <- fit_within(w)
  fr <- fit_within(w[anchortype == 1])
  ff <- fit_within(w[anchortype != 1])
  fa <- fit_across(cell_indices(a, sets$across_cells))
  data.table(model, rep, par = paste(names(par), unlist(par), sep = "=", collapse = ";"),
             b = fw$b, b_se = fw$b_se, g = fw$g, g_se = fw$g_se, rho = fw$rho, rho_se = fw$rho_se,
             b_random = fr$b, g_random = fr$g, g_random_se = fr$g_se, rho_random = fr$rho, rho_random_se = fr$rho_se,
             b_fixed = ff$b, g_fixed = ff$g, g_fixed_se = ff$g_se, rho_fixed = ff$rho, rho_fixed_se = ff$rho_se,
             across_slope = fa$slope, across_slope_se = fa$slope_se, across_mean_ai = fa$mean_ai)
}

jobs <- rbindlist(lapply(names(n_reps), function(m) data.table(model = m, rep = seq_len(n_reps[[m]]))))
res <- rbindlist(mclapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
  tryCatch(one_rep(jobs$model[i], jobs$rep[i]), error = function(e) data.table(model = jobs$model[i], rep = jobs$rep[i], error = conditionMessage(e)))
}, mc.cores = 8), fill = TRUE)
fwrite(res, file.path("output", "predictions_raw.csv"))

q <- function(v) paste0(sprintf("%.3f", median(v, na.rm = TRUE)), " [", sprintf("%.3f", quantile(v, .025, na.rm = TRUE)), ", ", sprintf("%.3f", quantile(v, .975, na.rm = TRUE)), "]")
summ <- res[is.na(if ("error" %in% names(res)) error else NA), .(reps = .N, b = q(b), g = q(g), rho = q(rho), g_random = q(g_random), g_fixed = q(g_fixed),
                                  rho_random = q(rho_random), rho_fixed = q(rho_fixed),
                                  b_random = q(b_random), b_fixed = q(b_fixed), across_slope = q(across_slope),
                                  across_mean_ai = q(across_mean_ai), share_g_pos = mean(g > 0)), by = model]
fwrite(summ, file.path("output", "predictions_summary.csv"))
print(summ)

summ <- res[is.na(if ("error" %in% names(res)) error else NA), .(reps = .N, b = q(b), g = q(g), rho = q(rho), g_random = q(g_random), g_fixed = q(g_fixed),
                                  rho_random = q(rho_random), rho_fixed = q(rho_fixed),
                                  b_random = q(b_random), b_fixed = q(b_fixed), across_slope = q(across_slope),
                                  across_mean_ai = q(across_mean_ai), share_g_pos = mean(g > 0)), by = model]
fwrite(summ, file.path("output", "predictions_summary.csv"))
print(summ)

# ---- Figure 1: model predictions at the median accepted calibration of each model --------------
calib <- fread(file.path("output", "calibration_grid.csv"))[accepted == TRUE]
med_par <- function(m) {
  g <- calib[model == m]
  keep <- names(which(sapply(g, function(v) !all(is.na(v)))))
  g <- g[, intersect(c("s", "t", "cost", "kappa", "w", "k", "c", "jk"), keep), with = FALSE]
  as.list(g[which.min(abs(jk - median(jk)))][, !"jk"])
}
set.seed(11)
grid <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.1)
f1 <- rbindlist(lapply(names(pal), function(m) {
  par <- med_par(m)
  data.table(model = m, x = grid, y = sapply(grid, function(x) {
    mu <- rnorm(20000, 0, belief_sd_share)
    mean(respond(m, rep(x, 20000), mu, 1, par))
  }))
}))
f1[, elasticity := c(NA, diff(y) / diff(x)), by = model]
f1[, elasticity := frollmean(elasticity, 7, align = "center"), by = model]
f1_long <- rbind(f1[, .(model, x, value = y, panel = "A. Mean estimate (log, relative to belief centre)")],
                 f1[, .(model, x, value = elasticity, panel = "B. Local elasticity (proportional pull)")])
p1 <- ggplot(f1_long, aes(x, value, colour = model, linetype = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal, name = NULL) + scale_linetype_manual(values = lt, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Anchor distance from the belief centre (log units, in SDs of belief uncertainty)", y = NULL) +
  theme_paper

# ---- Figure 2: observed within-item response functions -----------------------------------------
fits <- readRDS(file.path("output", "confirmatory", "fits.rds"))
source(file.path("R", "estimators.R"))
W <- drop_gross_errors(fits$W)
W[, bin := floor(x / 0.5)]   # fixed-width bins of 0.5 log units
binned <- W[, .(x = median(x), y = median(y), n = .N), by = .(cell, reference_short, anchortype, bin)][n >= 10]
m <- fits$h1$pooled$model
# Fitted curve for each cell (fixed effects plus that cell's random effects), over the central 95% of its anchors
curve <- W[, .(x = seq(quantile(x, .025), quantile(x, .975), length.out = 100)), by = .(cell)]
curve[, `:=`(xx = x * abs(x), pid = NA_character_)]
curve[, y := predict(m, newdata = curve, re.form = ~ (1 + x + xx || cell))]
W[, study_label := sprintf("%s (%s anchors)", reference_short, fifelse(anchortype == 1, "random", "fixed"))]
labs_cell <- unique(W[, .(cell, study_label)])
binned <- merge(binned, labs_cell, by = "cell")
curve <- merge(curve, labs_cell, by = "cell")
p2 <- ggplot(binned, aes(x, y)) +

# ---- Figure 3: across-cell index and Hedges' g against extremity --------------------------------
ci_A <- fits$ci_A
h2 <- fits$h2$model
e3 <- fread(file.path("output", "exploratory", "E3_hedges_g.csv"))
xs <- seq(min(ci_A$extremity), max(ci_A$extremity), length.out = 100)
pr <- predict(h2, newmods = xs)
line3 <- data.table(extremity = xs, est = pr$pred, lo = pr$ci.lb, hi = pr$ci.ub, panel = "A. Log anchoring index (preregistered, H2)")
pts <- rbind(ci_A[, .(extremity, value = ai, w = 1 / ai_se, panel = "A. Log anchoring index (preregistered, H2)")],
             e3[, .(extremity, value = g, w = 1 / sqrt(v), panel = "B. Hedges' g (exploratory)")])
m3 <- metafor::rma.mv(g, v, mods = ~ extremity, random = ~ 1 | study / cell, data = e3)
pr3 <- predict(m3, newmods = xs)

p3 <- ggplot(pts, aes(extremity, value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(size = w), shape = 21, fill = "grey70", colour = "white", stroke = 0.3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_ribbon(data = line3, aes(y = est, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = pal[["M1"]], alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(data = line3, aes(y = est), colour = pal[["M1"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3, guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Anchor extremity: mean |log(anchor / true value)| of the two anchors", y = NULL) +
  theme_paper
